Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System


Through 2050 the U.S. grid will rest on three jobs rather than three fuels: cheap energy, firm capacity and flexibility. This decade the scarce job is firm capacity that can actually connect, and policy should pay for the service a plant delivers.





Nov 3, 2026





No matching items

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
text: Several announcements in the past two weeks came with large headline numbers, and each carried a qualifier that matters more to anyone modeling new large loads and firm power. Below are five U.S. items and one from Europe, each with its primary source and my view of why it matters.

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
section: Exelon splits its data-center pipeline by maturity
text:
Exelon splits its data-center pipeline by maturity
What happened: In third-quarter materials filed on 30 October 2026, Exelon counted about 11 GW of data-center demand as high probability. These are projects in advanced design or backed by FERC-approved transmission security agreements. It listed a further future pipeline of about 23 GW, of which about 14 GW at its Illinois utility sits in current or future cluster studies that conclude in 2026 and 2027; the two groups should not be added together. Data-center load actually served in northern Illinois is still below 1 GW.
Why it matters (my view): Signed, studied and energized load are different quantities, and adding them together overstates near-term demand. In my work on delayed grid energization (CoDE), how long a project waits and whether it goes ahead can be linked, and the cost to ratepayers depended strongly on large-load tariff design. Disclosures by maturity level let a model treat these separately.
Source: Exelon Q3 2026 earnings presentation, slide 15 (SEC Form 8-K, Exhibit 99.2)

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
section: PJM tells FERC that flat data-center demand squeezes maintenance seasons
text:
PJM tells FERC that flat data-center demand squeezes maintenance seasons
What happened: At FERC’s reliability technical conference on 21 October 2026, PJM’s Christopher Pilong said that near-constant data-center demand makes reliability harder to keep in spring and fall, the seasons when generators and transmission owners usually take equipment out for maintenance. He likened it to “a rising sea level”. PJM’s prefiled statement asks for enforceable ride-through rules for large loads, and for energization decisions that allow for the time needed to build supply and transmission.
Why it matters (my view): Maintenance calendars are usually fixed model inputs, but with flat loads the shoulder season itself can become the binding constraint. Tying energization to supply build-out also creates exactly the wait that CoDE prices. In CoDE, staged service and bridge power are the main ways to recover value during that wait.
Source: PJM Inside Lines, 22 October 2026

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
text:
Gas-turbine backlogs keep growing
What happened: GE Vernova reported on 28 October 2026 that its gas power equipment backlog plus slot reservations reached 122 GW at the end of September, up from 116 GW a quarter earlier. It expects at least 130 GW by year-end. In the quarter, 13 GW of reservations became firm orders and 5 GW of equipment shipped.
Why it matters (my view): Models usually let a gas turbine appear in whatever year it is cheapest. A 122 GW pipeline against 5 GW of quarterly shipments argues for an explicit and uncertain lead time. For a large load that plans on-site gas as bridge power, the delivery slot can bind as tightly as the grid connection it stands in for.
Source: GE Vernova third-quarter 2026 results (SEC Form 8-K)

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
section: DOE offers up to $5 billion for Constellation nuclear uprates
text:
DOE offers up to $5 billion for Constellation nuclear uprates
What happened: On 27 October 2026, DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing made a conditional commitment to lend up to $5 billion for uprates and modernization at eight Constellation nuclear plants in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania. The work is expected to add nearly 1.1 GW in PJM and MISO. No money flows until Constellation meets technical, legal, environmental and financial conditions.
Why it matters (my view): An uprate adds firm, carbon-free capacity where the reactor’s capital is already sunk, so it behaves more like an add-on than a new build. My NPPH2 study found the same asymmetry for hydrogen. With the assumed credit, hydrogen revenue sustained most existing reactors studied but did not cover a new plant’s capital.
Source: U.S. Department of Energy, 27 October 2026

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
section: The EU reopens its hydrogen strategy
text:
The EU reopens its hydrogen strategy
What happened: On 26 October 2026, the European Commission opened a targeted consultation on a renewed hydrogen strategy. Authorities, industry, finance, NGOs and academia can respond until 23 November. The Commission is frank about the reason: six years after its 2020 strategy, little renewable or low-carbon hydrogen capacity is operating, and projects have been slow to mature.
Why it matters (my view): The gap between announced and operating capacity runs through this whole issue, on both sides of the Atlantic. In my NPPH2 work, market design, not only the plant, set the value of hydrogen flexibility. That makes a review of demand barriers and support design the place where model inputs are most likely to move.
Source: European Commission, consultation page

title: Briefing — 3 November 2026
section: ERCOT flags daylight-saving glitches in dashboard data
text:
ERCOT flags daylight-saving glitches in dashboard data
What happened: ERCOT warned on 30 October 2026 that the end of daylight saving time on 1 November would distort several public dashboards from 31 October to 2 November. Downloaded supply-and-demand files label hour ending 02 as 01, and the wind-and-solar series is empty for the repeated hour.
Why it matters (my view): These are display problems, not physical events, so a gap or a zero in that data is not an outage. Hourly series should be keyed to UTC or carry a daylight-saving flag, and such gaps should never be filled with zeros.
Source: ERCOT market notice M-B103026-01

text:

Will FERC and NERC turn large-load ride-through and interim, non-firm service into binding rules, and how soon?

text:
Mentoring
Mentored undergraduate researchers at The University of Texas at Dallas, 2022–2025, including through the Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) program. Their projects covered techno-economic analysis of renewable and hydrogen systems. In these projects, students moved from following a worked model to adapting it and defending their own assumptions.

title: Teaching
text:
Interactive explainers
Each explainer is a small interactive model on a project page that shows one mechanism from my research: move a slider and see why the result changes. They are designed to double as teaching material for techno-economic analysis, optimization and uncertainty quantification. The numbers are illustrative, not study results.

title: Hydrogen techno-economic parameters and inputs
text:
Reference data / Hydrogen
Source-specific hydrogen techno-economic parameters and inputs, preserving printed values, technical and monetary bases, source terms and paper cross-references. Includes historical status, design coefficients, targets, policy inputs, an observed retail price and a clearly labeled paper model assumption.
Version 0.1 Checked 2026-11-13 76 quantities
Download versioned CSV How to cite
U.S. focus, with the global IRENA synthesis labeled separately. Coverage: 2007/2031. 2007 cost bases through the 2031 Hydrogen Shot goal, including historical status and 2026 policy and market inputs. Ultimate technology targets are undated.
Not a harmonized forecast: values keep their sources’ bases. NR means not reported; BOL means beginning of life; NOAK means nth-of-a-kind. Blank numeric CSV fields are missing values, never zero. Records with suffixes separate quantities or applicable years while keeping their common H-number. Costs have not been escalated.
“Paper use or numerical correspondence” distinguishes a stated model assumption from a matching number. A matching number alone does not establish adoption of a source or technology classification. All expanded basis and locator text is present in the page and the downloads.

Read before using

Installed versus uninstalledEquipment, installed direct cost, total installed capital (TIC), total overnight cost (TOC) and total capital investment (TCI) have different inclusions. Apply installation factors only after checking the boundary.
Stack versus systemStack cost is part of system cost. Rectification and auxiliaries change electricity use; keep AC system input separate from DC stack ratings.
LHV versus HHVConsumption in kWh/kg is a physical ratio; lower or higher heating value defines an efficiency percentage. Electrical-only SOEC efficiency retains an additional heat input.
Capacity versus outputCost per kilogram stored, per kg/day of production capacity and per kilogram produced are different quantities.
Replacement versus O&MCheck replacement timing and inclusions before combining annual maintenance with per-replacement fractions or replacement-inclusive O&M.
Capture versus lifecycleProcess-carbon capture does not remove upstream methane, purchased-electricity or all combustion emissions. H52 is a reference-plant coefficient, not a lifecycle estimate.
Policy eligibility versus assumed supportA model’s support assumption does not establish statutory eligibility. Apply the production-year amount and the qualifying conditions together.
Production cost versus sale priceHydrogen Shot is a production-cost goal. Retail prices include downstream services; neither is automatically a plant-gate sale price.

Gaps
Public-source coverage still needed for comparable inputs:
ATR without CCSThe cited NETL report has no such case. Subtracting capture equipment from ATR+CCS does not supply a complete unabated design.
Unit-level CCS removal assumptionsNETL’s overall capture objective does not supply a universal solvent-removal input.
Before-capture intensity of capture-equipped plantsThe unabated SMR coefficient H52 should not be transferred to SMR+CCS or ATR+CCS; their fuel and process balances differ.
Current PEM/alkaline variable O&MA comparable public benchmark excluding electricity, water and stack replacement is not established here. H27 is a model factor.
Current MW-scale, continuous-duty pure-hydrogen fuel cellsInstalled CAPEX, variable O&M and lifetime require suitable public sources. Backup-system values and natural-gas CHP efficiencies are unsuitable substitutes.
Current storage and pipeline procurement costsHistorical DOE component benchmarks need newer public estimates with installation and location stated.
Hydrogen-only U.S. wholesale pricesH65 is a small retail sample. The BLS/FRED argon-and-hydrogen series is a combined index, not a hydrogen-only price per kilogram. Public reference
Additional California retail coverageThe CEC/CARB assessment is a further public reference; its numerical observations are not included in this edition. Public reference

title: Demand-side Management Under Real-time Greenhouse Gas Emission Factor for Electricity
text:
Gulai Shen, Honglin Li, Gurpreet Singh, Amir Behjat, Gerald Toge, Souroush Senemmar, Cong Feng, Jie Zhang, Ali Mehmani
2024 ACEEE Summer Study on Energy Efficiency in Buildings, 2024.
Abstract
Electric power generation contributes to the second largest share of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the US. The direct and indirect carbon emissions created from generating electricity vary from resources of generation, and power plant efficiency. Approximately 60% of the electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, mostly coal and natural gas, emitting more than 1500 million metric Tons of CO₂ per year. Depending on regions and time of day, the cleanness of electricity significantly varies as more and more intermittent renewable energy resources, such as solar and wind, being added into the grid. With the growing awareness and regulations on GHG emissions, the need for accurate carbon measurement and technologies that reduces GHG for both the supply and demand side is ever-increasing. To optimally control demand-side users such as buildings, balance supply and demand, and incorporate energy storage technologies to reduce overall GHG emissions, the real-time emission factor and its predictions play critical roles. Here, we use the open-source real-time electricity GHG Emission Factor that covers all states in the US and four sample buildings’ demand data from Nantum OS across different regions to propose an optimization framework for potential emission reduction through load shifting. This study highlights the importance to raise awareness, monitor, and account for real-time GHG emissions. Furthermore, it proves the viability to control buildings with electric energy storage system to reduce carbon emissions for demand-side users.

title: Techno-Economic Boundary Analysis of Small Modular Reactor Cogeneration for Hyperscale Data Center IT and Cooling Loads
text:
Honglin Li, Buxin She, Jie Zhang
Energy Conversion and Management, 2026. Accepted
Abstract
Hyperscale data centers are adding firm, high-utilization demand faster than grids can serve it, renewing interest in colocating them with small modular reactors. Such a plant could earn revenue in two ways, selling low-carbon power and diverting steam to absorption chillers that serve a cooling load accounting for 20-40% of facility electricity use, but neither revenue stream has been priced across the conditions that must coincide. Here we co-optimize reactor dispatch, steam extraction, absorption cooling and grid exchange hourly for a 200 MWₑ data center in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region, across 109 runs spanning capital, market, policy, financing and cooling efficiency. At 2023 mid-range reactor capital, the nuclear configurations cost 49-62% more than grid supply even with the Section 45Y production tax credit. The viable region opens near $5,000 kWₑ⁻¹, and nth-of-a-kind capital makes them 77-89% cheaper in 2023, though between parity and 34% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market. A carbon price of $53-64 tCO₂⁻¹ closes the mid-range gap under hourly export crediting. Absorption cooling is dispatched in response to hourly electricity prices and supplies 38% of annual cooling, at an added cost of $9.2 million yr⁻¹ relative to the reactor-only plant; that gap closes at an installed absorption cost of $60 kWc⁻¹ at baseline efficiency and $570 kWc⁻¹ on a legacy-efficiency campus, against surveyed commercial prices of $450-1,200 kWc⁻¹. Together these results delineate the capital, market and policy conditions under which colocated reactor cogeneration is competitive with grid procurement, and the range over which each condition moves the outcome.

title: Hydrogen’s role in expanding renewable energy and reducing carbon emissions in Texas
text:
Honglin Li, Jie Zhang
International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, vol. 113, pp. 77–89, 2025.
Abstract
Texas, with its substantial wind and solar capacities, plays a pivotal role in the U.S. strategy to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. Despite its leadership in wind energy generation and a growing solar sector, the integration of large-scale renewable energy in Texas faces significant challenges, primarily due to the intermittent nature of renewables and uncertainties surrounding future capacity expansion and demand growth. This study explores the potential of hydrogen as a solution to these challenges through a stochastic optimization model that accounts for the unpredictability of renewable energy installation timelines and fluctuations in electricity demand. The model designs a hydrogen network to mitigate geographical mismatches between energy supply and demand, providing a critical balancing mechanism. Our findings indicate that hydrogen can significantly enhance renewable energy penetration while reducing carbon emissions. Strategic placement of electrolyzers and hydrogen tanks, combined with inter-regional hydrogen transport, could satisfy up to 92.4% of hydrogen demand in certain regions. Additionally, annual hydrogen production across Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is projected to reach 131 tons, which corresponds to a carbon emissions reduction of 1,300 tons. Sensitivity analyses further reveal that higher electricity prices for combined cycle gas-turbine plants negatively impact the system’s overall energy efficiency, leading to an increase in carbon emissions. For instance, when electricity prices rise to $250 MWh⁻¹, annual system-wide carbon emissions increase by 310 kilotons compared to the benchmark scenario. This study highlights the critical role hydrogen can play in supporting Texas’s renewable energy ambitions and underscores the necessity for policy backing, investment, and advancements in both hydrogen and carbon capture technologies to fully realize its potential.

title: Techno-Economic Analysis of Hydrogen-Integrated Sustainable Energy Systems
text:
Honglin Li
Ph.D. dissertation, The University of Texas at Dallas, 2025.
Abstract
The global energy transition is driven by the urgent need to achieve deep decarbonization while maintaining system reliability and economic viability. Yet, the variability of renewable resources and the limited flexibility of conventional baseload power remain key barriers to large-scale integration. Hydrogen has emerged as a versatile solution, capable of providing long-duration storage, enabling sector coupling, and enhancing the operational flexibility of energy systems. This dissertation develops three distinct techno-economic analysis (TEA) frameworks that integrate optimization modeling with lifecycle financial evaluation to systematically assess hydrogen’s role in advancing sustainable energy systems. The study explores three interconnected applications. It first examines the integration of hydrogen storage with renewable generation, showing how co-location strategies reduce curtailment and improve cost-effectiveness under diverse market and resource conditions. It then broadens the scope to the grid level, using the Texas power system as a case study to evaluate how hydrogen can mitigate uncertainty in renewable deployment and demand growth, while inter-regional hydrogen networks alleviate geographic mismatches and contribute to significant carbon reductions. Building on these insights, the framework is applied to nuclear power systems, where hydrogen production enhances operational flexibility, supports participation in ancillary service markets, and creates new revenue streams—outcomes that are further reinforced under favorable policy incentives. These analyses illustrate hydrogen’s capacity to serve as a unifying energy carrier across renewable and nuclear contexts. The findings emphasize that the effectiveness of hydrogen-enabled systems depends not only on technological performance but also on evolving cost trajectories, market mechanisms, and policy frameworks. By establishing a coherent analytical foundation and offering actionable insights, this dissertation provides guidance for policymakers, industry leaders, and researchers in designing resilient, economically viable, and carbon-neutral energy pathways where hydrogen plays a central role.

title: Techno-economic analysis incorporating intelligent operation and maintenance management: a case study of an integrated offshore wind and hydrogen energy system
text:
Honglin Li, Mingxin Li, James Carroll, Jie Zhang
Journal of Physics: Conference Series, vol. 2767, article 062016, 2024.
Abstract
In this study, a comprehensive examination of wind-hydrogen energy systems is conducted through detailed techno-economic analysis and sensitivity analysis. The primary emphasis is on optimizing operation and maintenance (O&M) strategies and understanding the impacts of market dynamics. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we first identify the optimal intelligent O&M plan, leading to significant reductions in annual O&M costs ($39.9/MW) and downtime (6.59 days per turbine) compared to conventional methods. The incorporation of prognostics and health management (PHM) further demonstrate a notable impact, leading to a 9.9% reduction in O&M costs and a 10.7% decrease in downtime. In the broader context, these outcomes translate into reductions in the O&M expenditures, total lifecycle costs of the system, Levelized Cost of Hydrogen (LCOH) and Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) by 3.9%, 0.75%, 2.4%, and 1.8%, respectively, highlighting the economic benefits of intelligent O&M strategies. The extensive sensitivity analysis, encompassing 54 scenarios, delves into the effects of maintenance strategies, hydrogen prices, wind energy share, and subsidies, revealing nuanced insights into cost savings and operational efficiencies. Notably, intelligent maintenance and favorable hydrogen subsidies effectively reduce LCOH, while the interplay between wind energy share and hydrogen pricing influences system profitability and efficiency, underscoring the complex dynamics at play in optimizing renewable energy systems.

title: A Multi-Fidelity Gaussian Process Regression Method for Probabilistic Wind Farm Power Curve Estimation
text:
Honglin Li, Cong Feng, Jie Zhang
Proceedings of the ASME 2023 IDETC-CIE, Paper No. IDETC2023-114762, article V03AT03A034, 2023.
Abstract
Accurate estimation of the power curve for wind turbines or wind farms is crucial to ensure their efficient operation and management. However, conventional methods for power curve estimation rely either on expensive and infrequent measurements or on low-quality numerical simulations. Moreover, the majority of previous studies on power curve estimation for wind turbines or wind farms focused on deterministic estimation, which provides a point estimate of the relationship between wind speed and power generation. Nevertheless, the deterministic approach fails to consider the inherent uncertainty associated with wind energy production resulting from varying turbine characteristics. This can lead to inaccurate power generation estimation and suboptimal decisions regarding energy management. In this paper, a kernel density estimation (KDE) based Multi-Fidelity Gaussian Process Regression (MFGPR) model is proposed to fuse theoretical power curve data and the ground true measurements to create a mapping of wind speed and wind power. By conducting a case study on an actual wind farm in China, the efficacy of the proposed MFGPR model was demonstrated in characterizing the variability of wind power. The probabilistic MFGPR model was also able to generate confidence intervals that encompassed the measured power, thereby improving the accuracy and confidence in wind power estimation or wind resource assessment. Overall, the proposed MFGPR model offers a reliable approach to integrate high-fidelity ground measurements and theoretical power curve data, resulting in precise wind resource assessment and power estimation.

title: Facility and microgrid location-allocation for integrated supply chain and transactive energy operations
text:
Honglin Li, Tongdan Jin, Clara Novoa
Applied Mathematical Modelling, vol. 119, pp. 119–136, 2023.
Abstract
Supply chain network design usually focuses on the uncertainties in materials, capacity, yield, and demand. However, the challenges of prosumer energy integration are not adequately addressed. This paper proposes an integrated facility and microgrid location-allocation model for achieving low-carbon supply chain operations at the nexus of manufacturing, renewables, and climate. The model strategically locates the site for establishing factories, warehouses, and microgrids subject to product demand and energy supply uncertainty. The model further allocates production, inventory, transportation, generation, and energy transactions to lower the net supply chain cost. The study represents a first-of-its-kind in jointly siting and sizing industrial facilities and prosumer microgrids under a unified optimization framework. The proposed model is implemented in a three-tier production supply chain network over a one-year period, covering the US pacific region with broad climate conditions. Numerical experiments show that transactive energy, time-of-use tariff, and climate conditions play a critical role in locating factories, warehouses, wind turbines, solar photovoltaics, and energy storage systems. Since transactive energy market brings new revenue stream, locations with stronger renewables become competitive to establish facilities despite of higher fixed and logistics cost. Contrary to the intuition, energy storage systems, which balance the intermittent power and uncertain load, have limited benefits to the cost saving.

title: Planning Virtual Power Plants for Smart Factories and Industry 4.0 with Renewable and Thermal Cogeneration
text:
Honglin Li
M.S. thesis, Texas State University, 2021.
Abstract
Wind- and solar-based microgrid generation is a promising solution to reverse the climate change and achieve manufacturing sustainability. Virtual power plants (VPP) formed by a group of coordinated microgrid systems have the potential to accelerate the integration of variable renewable resources. We propose a facility-microgrid, location-allocation model to realize renewable and thermal cogeneration in smart factories and Industry 4.0. Under demand and supply uncertainty, the model jointly locates the factories and warehouse, assigns the transportation routes, and sizes wind turbines, photovoltaics, and energy storage for cost minimization. The model also performs operational planning for production, inventory, energy transactions, vehicle charging, and electricity and thermal cogeneration using combined heat and power. The proposed VPP planning model is demonstrated on multi-echelon supply chain networks using 11-year period, 2.3 million data. Several managerial insights are obtained. First, the experimental results show that the site with abundant renewables is opt for being the factory location despite of higher transportation and production cost. Second, the sizing of renewable microgrid is significantly influenced by time-of-use tariff or peaking price. Third, combined heat and power is proven to be a viable approach to streamline variable generation. Fourth, different decision-making criteria, such as value-at-risk and Minimax, may have huge impacts on the risk-averse planning. Future work can be focused on incorporating edge computing and vehicle-to-grid operations into the integration of renewable energy in smart factories.

title: Supply chain design for transactive energy operations in the nexus of manufacturing, microgrid and climate
text:
Tongdan Jin, Honglin Li, Siva Prashanth Kumar Prabha
Journal of the Operational Research Society, vol. 73, pp. 2395–2411, 2022.
Abstract
Manufacturing and supply chain sectors are undergoing a paradigm change driven by the growing use of distributed renewable energy. Under demand and generation uncertainty, this paper aims to allocate wind turbine, solar photovoltaics and energy storage units in a three-tier supply chain network to achieve sustainable operations with minimum cost. We propose a mixed-integer stochastic programming model that involves the production-inventory and microgrid capacity decisions along with the hourly energy transactions to meet the electrical loads of factories, warehouse, and retail stores. Our study advances existing supply chain design methods by explicitly incorporating transactive energy, materials, information and cash flows into a holistic optimization framework. The performance and scalability of the model is tested in two network instances with various facility locations, machine capacity, and climate conditions. Results show that onsite renewable generation enables large industrial consumers to achieve environmental sustainability as well as to create new revenue stream through the participation in transactive energy market. The study also indicates that feed-in tariff, time-of-use rate, two-way energy trading can lower the utility cost and accelerate the adoption of variable generation technology.

title: Integrating offshore wind farms with unmanned hydrogen and battery ships
text:
Sobhan Badakhshan, Soroush Senemmar, Honglin Li, Jie Zhang
2022 IEEE Kansas Power and Energy Conference (KPEC), pp. 1–6, 2022.
Abstract
The transition to low-carbon electrical grids has enabled a rapid growth in offshore wind energy. In the meantime, producing green hydrogen from offshore wind farms has also gained wide attention in recent years. Among many challenges, energy transferring from offshore wind farms (especially for those in deep water) to the shoreline infrastructure has been explored in various ways. In this paper, unmanned surface hydrogen ships are explored as mobile energy resources to replace hydrogen pipelines to transfer hydrogen generated from offshore wind farms in deep water, in conjunction with unmanned battery ships for electricity transmission. The hydrogen/battery ships could charge from offshore wind farms and discharge their energy when plugged-in to the terrestrial grid or onshore hydrogen infrastructure. The schedules of the ships are optimized based on the offshore wind farm generation, weather conditions, and ship sailing timing. Results showed that by combining the hydrogen ship, battery ship, and onsite hydrogen storage tanks, more than 99% of the offshore wind farm generation could be successfully transmitted to the shore side infrastructure.

title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian processes for wind power curves
text:
ProjectsWind uncertainty





First author
Open SDWPF SCADA dataNine test turbinesKernel density samplingMulti-fidelity Gaussian processesPoint and probabilistic metrics


Research question
Can multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression, combining a theoretical power curve with limited measured data, improve probabilistic wind turbine power-curve estimation?


Key insight
A theoretical power curve helped, but the gain depended on the metric
The method fuses about two hundred sampled measurements with the theoretical power curve of the turbine type, which covers all wind speeds but does not show how a turbine actually runs. In the reported nine-turbine test, nonlinear multi-fidelity regression had a lower RMSE than standard Gaussian process regression for most turbines, but the ranking depended on the evaluation metric.


How does a theoretical curve help a few measurements?

A Gaussian process fitted to a few measured points is uncertain wherever the points are sparse, so its band widens between them. A multi-fidelity model also learns from the turbine's theoretical power curve, which covers every wind speed, and uses it to fill in the shape between measurements, so the band can narrow there. In the paper's test, the result depended on the evaluation metric.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I implemented and evaluated the models and did the writing, with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy through the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.


How I approached it

ChallengeMeasured SCADA records show real behavior, including scatter, stops and curtailment, but are noisy and very numerous.What I didI drew a few hundred representative points from a kernel density estimate of the records, which keeps the shape of the scatter without manual cleaning.Why it matteredA Gaussian process solve grows with the cube of the training points, so a compact training set matters.
ChallengeThe theoretical curve covers every wind speed but not how a turbine actually operates.What I didI compared linear and nonlinear multi-fidelity models, which link the curve to the measurements, with a standard Gaussian process on measurements alone, on point and probabilistic metrics.Why it matteredTesting both kinds of metric showed that the gain depended on which error matters.



Method
Linear (autoregressive) and nonlinear multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression that fuse the turbine type's theoretical power curve (low fidelity) with a few hundred kernel-density-sampled SCADA points from the open SDWPF dataset (high fidelity), compared with single-fidelity regression on point and probabilistic metrics.


Key findings

In the reported nine-turbine test, nonlinear multi-fidelity regression achieved lower RMSE for most turbines; performance depended on the evaluation metric.



Boundary conditions
One dataset and one generic low-fidelity curve.

title: Co-located solar and hydrogen plants
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
115-MW solar plantWest Texas siteThree design casesREopt linked to SAMMILP sizing and dispatch


Research question
Is concentrated solar power with thermal storage feeding high-temperature electrolysis more economic than photovoltaics feeding low-temperature electrolysis in West Texas?


Key insight
With cheap thermal storage, a variable-power electrolyzer gave the lowest hydrogen cost
Among the cases studied, concentrated solar power with thermal storage, running a high-temperature electrolyzer at variable power, gave the lowest levelized cost of hydrogen; holding the electrolyzer at constant power was the most expensive. The paper attributes the advantage of concentrated solar mainly to the low cost of thermal energy storage.


My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I added a concentrated-solar module to the REopt-based model, ran the analysis and did the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeThe REopt-based model had no concentrated solar power or high-temperature electrolysis.What I didI simulated the solar field and tower with NREL's System Advisor Model and linked it to REopt through PySAM, adding an electrolyzer whose heat and electricity needs are met from the plant's output.Why it matteredOne optimization could then size the electrolyzer and thermal storage and plan their dispatch in each case.



Design choices

Run the photovoltaic case without a batteryAlternatives considered: photovoltaics with battery storageA battery would not be cost-effective when hydrogen can be stored downstream, and low-temperature electrolyzers tolerate fluctuating input better than high-temperature ones.



Method
Optimization of a 115-MW solar plant with electrolysis using SAM solar models, ERCOT prices and ATB cost trajectories.


Key findings

Among the cases studied, concentrated solar power with thermal storage running the electrolyzer at variable power gave the lowest levelized hydrogen cost; constant-power operation was the most expensive.



Boundary conditions
Single West Texas site; cost trajectories from NREL's Annual Technology Baseline; conference-length study.


What it led to
The same plant-scale optimization next went offshore, linked to a simulation of wind-farm maintenance. Intelligent operation and maintenance in offshore wind–hydrogen systems

title: Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





First author
200 MWe data center, ERCOTBWRX-300 reactor8,760 hours109 scenario runsHourly MILP co-optimization


Research question
Under which reactor-capital, market and policy conditions can a small modular reactor colocated with a hyperscale data center, and using its steam to drive absorption cooling, supply the campus more cheaply than the grid?


Key insight
An output-based credit makes cooling with reactor steam more expensive
The Section 45Y credit is paid per megawatt-hour of electricity. Steam sent to the absorption chiller is steam the low-pressure turbine does not convert, so each unit of cooling heat gives up both power and the credit on it. The incentive that narrows the reactor's capital gap also raises the cost of recovering its heat.


Why does the credit discourage steam cooling?

Reactor steam can either drive the turbine or feed an absorption chiller that makes chilled water. The production tax credit pays only for electricity. Every unit of steam sent to the chiller lowers turbine output and forfeits the credit on that output. So a larger credit raises the price at which steam cooling pays, leaving more hours to the electric chiller.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I co-conceived the study, co-developed the methodology, wrote the model software, curated the data, ran the analysis, made the figures and wrote the original draft.


How I approached it

ChallengeThe value of steam cooling depends on hourly physics: wet-bulb derating, crystallization risk, part-load chiller efficiency and the turbine work lost to extraction.What I didI modeled how each chiller's performance changes with weather and load, and how much turbine power is lost when steam goes to cooling: absorption performance against hourly wet-bulb temperature with a crystallization cutoff, the electric chiller's part-load curve with SOS2 constraints, and extraction with a Willans-line penalty from a steam-table heat balance.Why it matteredPricing diverted steam matters: treating it as a free by-product can by itself decide the sign of a cogeneration result.
ChallengeOne-at-a-time sensitivities cannot show whether a project falls inside the region where colocation beats the grid.What I didI designed 109 scenario runs, a baseline and nine sensitivity groups, including a five-by-five grid of reactor and absorption-chiller capital costs and a grid of reactor capital by market year.Why it matteredThe joint grid placed grid parity near $5,000/kWe under 2023 prices and showed that chiller capital moves the margin by at most 13 points.
ChallengeOne BWRX-300 produces about 2.9 times the campus's average IT load, so the plant is partly a merchant generator.What I didI swept campus size from 0.5 to 3.0 times the IT load, with the reactor fixed and the grid connection enlarged only for campuses above the baseline size.Why it matteredSize matching explained part of the gap, not most: the cogeneration margin improved from −62% to −29% at three times the load.
ChallengeMargins measured against grid cost are distorted across market years, because the grid cost itself falls in low-price years.What I didI reported cross-year results also in absolute annualized cost, next to the grid-cost margin.Why it matteredIn absolute terms the market year moved the cogeneration cost by about $48 million a year, a fifth of the reactor-capital range.



Design choices

Extract steam at the high- to low-pressure turbine crossoverAlternatives considered: a parallel tap on main steamCrossover steam has already expanded through the high-pressure turbine, so it costs about half as much turbine work; a sweep of the penalty tests this assumption.
Keep a full-size electric chiller and let both chillers share dispatchAlternatives considered: absorption as the primary chiller, with electric backup for emergencies onlyThe absorber has no steam during refueling and runs mainly in high-price hours, so the optimizer chooses between the chillers hour by hour.
Levelize the ten-year 45Y credit over the 20-year comparison windowAlternatives considered: levelizing it over the reactor's 40-year lifeThis matches the credit to the annualized-cost comparison; the 40-year variant moves the thresholds but not the mechanism.



Method
The model compares supplying a data center's electricity and cooling from a colocated reactor with buying from the grid or running an on-site gas plant, and works out hour by hour how each option would run. In technical terms: a mixed-integer linear program that co-optimizes, for every hour of a year, reactor output, steam extraction at the turbine crossover, absorption and electric cooling, and grid exchange for a 200 MWe data center in Houston (ERCOT) colocated with a BWRX-300 reactor; grid supply and an on-site gas combined cycle are evaluated on the same hourly basis. 109 scenario runs vary reactor and chiller capital cost, market year (2022–2024), carbon price, cost of capital, cooling efficiency, battery storage and campus size, with the Section 45Y production tax credit as the baseline policy.


Key findings

At 2023 ERCOT prices and mid-range reactor capital cost (ATB 2024), the nuclear configurations cost 49–62% more than grid supply, even with the Section 45Y credit.
Grid parity at zero carbon price requires reactor capital near $5,000/kWe under 2023 prices. At nth-of-a-kind capital the nuclear options are 77–89% cheaper than grid supply in 2023, but between parity and 34% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market.
A carbon price of $53–64 per tonne of CO₂ closes the mid-range gap when exports are credited at the hourly average grid emission intensity.
Absorption cooling follows hourly electricity prices and supplies 38% of annual cooling, but adds $9.2 million per year relative to the reactor-only plant; it breaks even only at an installed chiller cost near $60/kWc ($570/kWc on a legacy-efficiency campus), against surveyed prices of $450–1,200/kWc.
Capital cost and policy set the boundary; operating choices move it far less. Across the tested ranges, reactor capital spans 321 percentage points of the grid-cost margin and the cost of capital 119, against 12, 13 and 1 for cooling efficiency, chiller capital and battery storage.



Boundary conditions
One colocation-style load profile at one Houston site; hourly average rather than marginal emission factors, with the carbon-price crossovers conditional on crediting exports; demand charges and ancillary-service revenues excluded; reliability not modeled on a common basis across options; the reactor is one fixed commercial unit. The numerical thresholds depend on these market, financing and crediting conventions; the mechanism does not.


What it led to
The same question also matters at the national scale, which is the subject of my next study. Data-center demand and the commercialization of small modular reactors

title: UQ metrics and surrogate models for plant-level wind power
text:
ProjectsWind uncertainty





Research question
Can uncertainty metrics of a wind power model's inputs (weather data products, forecast ensembles and turbine-level data) predict calibrated plant-level power uncertainty at wind plants that have no power measurements?


My contribution
Ph.D. researcher on The University of Texas at Dallas part of the project. I developed the surrogate-modeling workflow (calibrated uncertainty targets, surrogate models and validation on held-out plants) and implemented the project's uncertainty metrics in Python, with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy through the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.


Method
The workflow learns, at wind plants with power measurements, how the uncertainty of a plant's power forecast relates to measures of uncertainty in its inputs, and uses that relation to estimate forecast uncertainty at plants without measurements. In technical terms: moving-window, data-source, ensemble-spread and spatial (variogram) uncertainty metrics as inputs; pinball-loss-optimal scales of a predictive distribution around the point forecast as targets at observed plants; Gaussian process regression and other regressors as surrogates; validation by holding out whole plants, scored with pinball loss, CRPS and reliability, with recalibration of the predictive distributions.


Boundary conditions
No paper. The public framework is a fresh implementation, tested on synthetic data and on a public benchmark of 264 ERCOT wind plants (ARPA-E PERFORM data, simulated plant power, 2018); project data and results are not public.




Outputs

Model framework (GitHub)
Public-data case study (GitHub)

title: The cost of delayed energization for AI data centers
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





First author
Present-value frameworkDeveloper, ratepayer, social ledgersIllustrative 300 MW-IT caseLatin hypercube screeningStaged service, bridge power


Research question
What does it cost when a large AI data center must wait for grid energization, and how does the delay affect the developer, electricity ratepayers and society?


Key insight
The cost of delayed energization depends on who is counting
A late grid connection costs the developer lost margin and carrying costs; ratepayers face utility carrying and stranding costs; society bears external costs. I keep these present-value accounts separate. In the study's illustrative base case, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion, while ratepayer exposure depended strongly on large-load tariff design.


My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the framework, the model, the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeDelay costs fall on different parties, and a single total hides who pays.What I didI priced the delay in three separate present-value ledgers (developer, utility ratepayers and society) with a net-benefit test that states when they may be combined.Why it matteredAn acceleration option can then be judged against what it saves each party and what it costs.
ChallengeDelay costs of projects with different sizes and waits are hard to compare.What I didI defined two metrics: a delay cost intensity per MW-month, and a break-even acceleration payment for options that shorten the wait.Why it matteredThey make results comparable across project sizes, delays and mitigation options such as staged service or bridge power.
ChallengeInputs are uncertain, and the length of a delay and whether a project goes ahead may be linked.What I didI screened inputs with Latin hypercube sampling and rank correlations, and stress-tested the dependence between delay and realization and the large-load tariff.Why it matteredThe parameters are illustrative, so the study reports which inputs move the result, not a single forecast.



Design choices

Treat the delay as givenAlternatives considered: modeling the interconnection process that causes itThe framework prices the consequences of late service; why service is late, and network feasibility, are outside its scope.



Method
Present-value framework that converts delayed IT capacity into grid capacity requirements and prices the delay in separate developer, ratepayer and social ledgers, summarized by a delay cost intensity and a break-even acceleration payment; sensitivity and dependence stress tests.


Key findings

In the study's illustrative base case, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion in present value.
Staged energization can recover a large share of that cost.
Ratepayer exposure depends strongly on large-load tariff design.



Boundary conditions
The delay is treated as exogenous and parameters are illustrative; network feasibility is not modeled, and the social perspective is illustrated with a single bridge-power example.

title: Honglin Li (李洪林)
text:
Honglin Li (李洪林)
      Postdoctoral Fellow Electrical and Computer Engineering Kansas State University
    

    
      I am an energy systems researcher and a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
        at Kansas State University. I build optimization and techno-economic models that show which low-carbon technology
        mixes deliver reliable, affordable energy, and who pays for them. My doctoral research asked when flexibility, from
        hydrogen or from demand, adds value to a low-carbon energy system, at the scale of a plant, a state and the U.S. nuclear
        fleet. My current research asks how large new electricity loads such as AI data centers can be supplied with firm,
        low-carbon power, including small modular reactors.
      My methods include linear, mixed-integer, nonlinear, stochastic and multi-objective optimization, combined with life
        cycle cost and carbon footprint analysis, simulation and reliability modeling. Applications span wind, solar and
        hydrogen systems, regional hydrogen networks, nuclear–hydrogen integration, small modular reactors for data centers,
        grid integration of data centers, and energy storage. My first-author papers appear in Nature Communications,
        Cell Reports Sustainability and the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, with one accepted in Energy Conversion and Management.

title: Supply chains with on-site microgrids and transactive energy
text:
ProjectsMicrogrids & supply chains





First author (AMM, SEGRE)
Multi-tier supply chainOn-site wind, solar, storageHourly grid buying and selling52 weeks of 168 hoursMixed-integer location model


Research question
Where should a manufacturing supply chain place its facilities, and how much on-site wind, solar and storage should each facility install when facilities can trade energy with the grid?


Key insight
With on-site renewables, wind and sun become part of the siting decision
When each facility can install its own wind, solar and storage and trade energy with the grid, a candidate site's renewable resource affects its operating cost. The model then weighs transport cost against resource quality, and storage became worthwhile under high peak prices or capped grid imports.


My contribution
First author of the location-allocation papers (AMM, SEGRE), for which I did most of the work. Second author of the JORS paper, for which I contributed to the optimization models and the case-study analyses.


How I approached it

ChallengeWhere a facility opens decides its wind and solar resource, while transport, production and energy costs depend on the same decisions.What I didWith my co-authors, I developed a mixed-integer model that opens factories and warehouses, routes products and sizes each open site's wind, solar and storage, with an hourly energy balance and grid trade.Why it matteredSolving these together showed that facility siting trades transport cost against renewable resource quality.
ChallengeWeekly store demand is uncertain, yet the network has to meet it reliably.What I didI modeled demand as a chance constraint with a set service level, written as its deterministic equivalent.Why it matteredThe model stays a mixed-integer linear program while holding the chance of a stock-out to the chosen level.



Method
JORS sizes on-site microgrids for fixed facility locations with production and inventory planning; AMM and SEGRE add facility location-allocation decisions.


Key findings

Facility siting trades transport cost against renewable resource quality (AMM).
On-site renewables lower total supply-chain cost under the modeled time-of-use tariffs.
In the AMM price scenarios, batteries became attractive at high peak electricity prices; in JORS, capping grid imports made storage worthwhile.



Boundary conditions
Stylized multi-echelon networks with synthetic distances and costs.

text:
ProjectsCarbon-aware grid





First author
12 U.S. grid regionsHourly EIA data, 2023Mixed-integer load regulationMonth, quarter, year windowsThree case studies


Research question
How much do the emissions attributed to electricity consumption fall when load is re-timed according to hourly average grid emission intensity across U.S. regions, and which strategies suit which types of grid?


Key insight
Shifting load toward cleaner hours cuts attributed emissions only modestly
Because total use in each window cannot fall, emissions drop only through the gap in intensity between hours, and the allowed range limits how much load can move. In the reported scenarios, reductions were on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less, largest with longer windows and wider ranges in renewable-rich, diverse grids.


How much can re-timing load cut emissions?

Each hour of the grid has an average emission intensity. The model moves part of the load from high-intensity hours to low-intensity hours in the same window, within an allowed range, and keeps total use unchanged. Attributed emissions fall by the load moved times the intensity gap between those hours. Because the range is limited, the reduction is modest; it grows with a wider range and a longer window.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the methodology, data processing, optimization modeling, analysis and writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeGrid regions differ in renewable share, generation mix and intensity swings, so one strategy cannot fit all.What I didI helped group the regions by renewable penetration, generation diversity and intensity fluctuation, and tested one strategy dimension on each: window length, adjustment range and adjustment penalty.Why it matteredThis showed which strategies suit which types of grid, the question the study set out to answer.
ChallengeRe-timing load inconveniences users, which an emissions-only objective ignores.What I didI helped add a penalty on each adjusted hour, counted with a binary variable, and varied its weight.Why it matteredIt revealed that regions with low intensity fluctuation are more sensitive to the cost of regulating load.



Design choices

Re-time load without reducing total useAlternatives considered: also allowing demand reductionEmissions then fall only because load moves to cleaner hours, so the study isolates the value of timing.



Method
Mixed-integer load-regulation model solved for each optimization cycle (month, quarter or year): hourly load moves toward lower-intensity hours within an allowed adjustment range, without lowering the cycle's total consumption, and each adjusted hour carries a penalty. Applied to U.S. grid regions with EIA hourly data (2023), varying the cycle, the adjustment range and the penalty, and grouping regions by renewable penetration, generation diversity and intensity fluctuation.


Key findings

Longer optimization windows and wider adjustment ranges increase the reduction in attributed emissions, most in renewable-rich and diverse grids.
In the reported scenarios, reductions in attributed emissions are modest, on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less.
Regions with low intensity fluctuation are more sensitive to the cost of regulating load.



Boundary conditions
Reductions are computed under average-emission-intensity accounting with perfect foresight; they are not estimates of the consequential (marginal) system response.

title: Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
42 reactors7 ISO/RTO marketsHourly MILP dispatchLifetime cash-flow analysis2024 market prices


Research question
Can existing and new U.S. nuclear power plants improve their economics and operating flexibility by adding high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen storage and batteries, and by selling energy, hydrogen and ancillary services?


Key insight
With the assumed hydrogen credit, hydrogen revenue can sustain an existing reactor but not pay for a new one
The study treats an existing reactor's capital as already spent. At 2024 prices, without capacity payments or the 45U credit, electricity sales alone left nearly all reactors below zero net present value; adding hydrogen and reserves, with the assumed $3/kg hydrogen credit for ten years, lifted most above zero. A new plant must also recover the reactor's capital cost, and new builds stayed below zero even with tax credits.


Why does hydrogen help an existing reactor more than a new one?

A reactor earns from electricity; with an electrolyzer it can also sell hydrogen and offer reserves, and a hydrogen production credit adds to that. The study treats an existing reactor's capital as already spent, so these revenues need to cover operating costs and the new equipment. A new plant must also recover the reactor's capital cost, and in the study the same revenues did not cover it.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the methodology, the optimization and lifetime techno-economic models (developed during my internship at Idaho National Laboratory), the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeSeven U.S. markets price energy and ancillary services differently, and each of 42 reactors faces its own prices.What I didI co-developed an hourly dispatch model that co-optimizes electricity sales, hydrogen production, storage and ancillary services under each market's products, run for every reactor.Why it matteredIt showed how market design, not only the reactor, shapes the value of flexibility.
ChallengeElectrolyzers and turbines are not ideal: efficiency varies with load, starts wear equipment, and ramping is limited.What I didI helped represent turbine and electrolyzer efficiency with piecewise-linear curves, track electrolyzer degradation from operation and start-ups, and enforce ramp limits and minimum stable load.Why it matteredFlexibility estimates then respect what the equipment can actually do.
ChallengeOne year of hourly dispatch had to become a lifetime investment case under several federal credits.What I didI co-developed a discounted cash-flow model with component-level capital costs, scheduled replacements and the 45U, 45V-type, 45Y and 48E credits, linked to the dispatch results.Why it matteredThe same operation could be judged as a retrofit (with and without 45U) or as a new build (no credit, 45Y or 48E); the hydrogen credit is assumed throughout.



Design choices

Take electricity and hydrogen prices as given (price-taking)Alternatives considered: equilibrium or game-theoretic market models with price feedbackThe study evaluates plant operation against observed 2024 prices; price feedback from wide adoption is stated as a limit and left to future work.



Method
Hourly mixed-integer optimization of turbine, electrolyzer and storage dispatch for 42 reactors in seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets using 2024 prices, linked to a lifetime cash-flow model with federal tax credits (45U, a 45V-type hydrogen credit, 45Y and 48E).


Key findings

Operated as electricity-only baseload plants at 2024 market prices, without capacity payments or the 45U nuclear credit, nearly all reactors studied had negative net present value.
With hydrogen integration and the assumed hydrogen production credit ($3/kg for ten years), a majority of the reactors reached positive net present value, even without the 45U credit.
Integrated operation added output flexibility; ancillary-service revenue was a few percent of the total.
For new builds, investment and production tax credits substantially lowered the levelized cost of hydrogen.



Boundary conditions
Results rely on 2024 prices, price-taking market participation, modeled ancillary-service participation parameters, the assumed hydrogen credit ($3/kg for ten years, applied in every scenario) and a dispatch held fixed after the credit expires. Capacity-market revenues and price feedback from large-scale adoption are not modeled, and the electricity-only baseline is stated without the 45U nuclear credit.


What it led to
New plants did not pay for themselves here, which raised the question of what could cover a new reactor's capital cost; AI data centers are the candidate buyer my next studies examine. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center

title: Intelligent operation and maintenance in offshore wind–hydrogen systems
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
Gulf of Mexico wind areaHouston refinery hydrogen demandMonte Carlo maintenance simulationTwo-stage optimization54 sensitivity scenarios


Research question
How much does prognostics-based operation and maintenance change the cost of an offshore wind farm supplying electrolytic hydrogen?


Key insight
A large maintenance saving became a small hydrogen-cost saving
In the simulated case study, prognostics-based maintenance lowered wind operation-and-maintenance cost by about 10% and downtime by about 11%. The saving applies to the turbines alone, so its effect on the whole system was smaller: the modeled levelized cost of hydrogen fell by about 2%.


My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I linked an operation-and-maintenance simulation, developed with my co-authors, to the system techno-economic optimization, ran the analysis and did the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeMaintenance strategy and system design were optimized in separate models.What I didI took the expected maintenance cost and turbine downtime from the maintenance optimization and used them as inputs to the system sizing and dispatch model.Why it matteredThis traced the effect of maintenance through to the levelized costs of hydrogen and electricity.
ChallengeAn offshore hydrogen plant needs a realistic site, buyer and price signal.What I didI placed the system in a federal Gulf of Mexico wind energy area, estimated Houston-area refinery hydrogen demand from the capacities of ten refineries, and used Houston load-zone prices.Why it matteredThis tied the case study to a designated site and an existing demand center.



Design choices

Apply prognostics-based maintenance only to the wind turbinesAlternatives considered: applying it to the hydrogen equipment as wellCondition monitoring and prognostics are more mature for offshore wind than for hydrogen assets.



Method
Two-stage approach: Monte Carlo operation-and-maintenance simulation, then techno-economic optimization for a Gulf of Mexico site supplying Houston-area refineries.


Key findings

In the simulated case study, prognostics-based maintenance lowered wind operation-and-maintenance cost by about 10% and downtime by about 11%.
At the system level, the modeled levelized cost of hydrogen fell by about 2%.



Boundary conditions
Single site and one weather year; maintenance parameters from the collaborators' framework.


Related regional study
These plant studies took the site as given. My Texas study works at the scale of a whole grid: it asks where hydrogen assets should be built and how hydrogen should move between zones. Hydrogen's role in expanding renewable energy in Texas

title: Small modular reactors for data centers
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





Co-first author
Perspective articleTechno-economic sectionFOAK and NOAK costsReliability premiumLevelized cost of computing


Research question
What would it take for small modular reactors to power data centers, and which economic dimensions must a credible techno-economic assessment capture?


Key insight
Reliability requirements add a capital premium that levelized cost leaves out
For a campus that targets Tier IV-level availability, one reactor alone cannot ride through refueling and unplanned outages. In the Perspective's N+1 example, a 300 MW campus needs 400 MW of SMR capacity: one 100 MW module more than the load. Standard levelized-cost estimates omit this reliability premium, so they understate the cost of firm on-site supply.


My contribution
Co-first author. Wrote the techno-economic analysis section, introduction and conclusions.


How I approached it

ChallengePublished SMR cost figures mix first-of-a-kind budgets with long-run nth-of-a-kind targets.What I didI set first-of-a-kind and nth-of-a-kind capital costs of SMR projects side by side and argued that assessments treat them as separate cases, each with its own financing and risk.Why it matteredLong-run figures make first projects look more viable than they are, and early data-center buyers carry that risk.
ChallengeLevelized cost of electricity leaves out cooling, which takes 30–40% of a hyperscale facility's energy.What I didIn the section I drafted, I proposed a service-based metric, the levelized cost of computing, which puts electricity and cooling costs over units of computing service.Why it matteredIt compares on-site nuclear, grid and renewable-plus-storage supply by what each delivers to the data center.



Method
Perspective synthesizing technology, economics and policy for SMR-powered data centers.


Key findings

Data-center reliability requirements add a substantial premium to the capital cost of on-site nuclear supply.
First-of-a-kind and nth-of-a-kind cost estimates for SMRs diverge widely, so assumptions must be explicit.
Service-based metrics, such as cost per unit of computing, and co-products such as heat matter for comparisons.



Boundary conditions
A Perspective: it frames the questions and evidence rather than presenting a new case-study model.


What it led to
Pricing the heat used for cooling, hour by hour, became the core of my boundary analysis for one data-center campus. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center

title: Hydrogen’s role in expanding renewable energy in Texas
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
8 ERCOT weather zones8,760 hours9 scenariosTwo-stage stochastic LPInter-zonal hydrogen pipelines


Research question
Where should electrolyzers, hydrogen storage and fuel cells be built in ERCOT, and how should hydrogen move between zones, to absorb surplus renewable generation and supply industrial hydrogen demand under uncertain 2030 renewable build-out?


Key insight
Dearer gas power diverted green hydrogen to power generation and raised emissions
When gas-fired backup power became much more expensive, the model built fuel cells and turned stored green hydrogen back into electricity. Industry then drew more hydrogen from gas reformers, and the round trip from power to hydrogen and back lost energy, so total emissions rose although gas-plant emissions fell.


How can dearer gas power raise emissions?

When gas-fired backup power becomes more expensive, the model starts to use stored green hydrogen in fuel cells to make electricity in hours of low wind and sun. That hydrogen no longer supplies industry, so gas reformers fill the gap with fossil hydrogen. Converting electricity to hydrogen and back loses energy, so in the paper's high-price cases total emissions rose even though emissions from gas plants fell.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the data pipeline from public ERCOT market disclosures, the stochastic planning model, the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeThe model needed hourly wind and solar output for each of ERCOT's eight weather zones.What I didI built it from ERCOT's 60-day market disclosures: each wind and solar resource mapped to its county and zone, averaged to hours, gap-filled and summed, then turned into zone capacity factors.Why it matteredThe same capacity factors scaled planned capacity from the interconnection queue, so existing and future renewables shared one hourly basis.
ChallengeHow much planned renewable capacity is built by 2030, and how fast demand grows, are both uncertain.What I didI formulated a two-stage stochastic program: hydrogen equipment is sized once, then operated hour by hour in nine scenarios combining three completion rates and three demand levels.Why it matteredThe sizes minimize expected cost over all nine scenarios instead of fitting a single forecast.
ChallengeWind and solar output is concentrated far from electricity demand in the north and southeast, and from hydrogen demand on the Gulf Coast.What I didI added hydrogen pipelines between adjacent weather zones, with transport cost set by the distance between zone centers.Why it matteredThe model could then choose between making hydrogen near surplus power and moving it, or making it where it is used.



Design choices

Hold hydrogen demand fixed across scenariosAlternatives considered: treating hydrogen demand as a third uncertain factorReliable hydrogen-demand data were lacking and computational cost mattered; the paper names this as future work.
Move hydrogen only by pipeline between neighboring zonesAlternatives considered: adding truck or rail transportPipelines are the relevant mode for large-scale, long-term deployment; other modes were left out to keep the focus on supply and demand uncertainty.



Method
Two-stage stochastic linear program. The first stage sizes electrolyzers, hydrogen tanks and fuel cells in each of ERCOT's eight weather zones; the second stage schedules batteries, electrolysis, fuel cells, gas-fired backup, reformer hydrogen and inter-zonal hydrogen transport hour by hour over a full year, in nine scenarios (three electricity-demand levels by three completion rates of planned renewable capacity). Inputs are built from ERCOT 60-day SCED disclosures, the LBNL interconnection queue and EIA data.


Key findings

Renewable (green) hydrogen covered only a few percent of industrial hydrogen demand; reformer hydrogen remained the main supply.
Modest load flexibility (±5%) reduced CO₂ emissions from combined-cycle gas generation.



Boundary conditions
Inputs reflect 2022–2023 conditions; post-2023 federal hydrogen credit rules are not modeled.


What it led to
Next I asked the same flexibility question of firm low-carbon supply: whether hydrogen production can make existing nuclear plants more flexible and profitable. Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants

title: Co-located wind and hydrogen energy systems
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
253-MW wind farm, Texas8,760 hoursFour system configurationsMILP (REopt extension)Four ISO wind profiles


Research question
How do electrolyzers, hydrogen storage and fuel cells change the cost, curtailment and firm output of a grid-connected wind farm?


Key insight
A higher hydrogen price raised hydrogen's levelized cost but lowered system cost
As the hydrogen price rose, the optimizer built a larger electrolyzer to use more surplus wind. The larger unit ran at lower utilization, so each kilogram carried more capital and the levelized cost of hydrogen rose, while hydrogen revenue lowered total system cost. The cost per kilogram and the system's cost moved in opposite directions.


Why can a costlier kilogram mean a cheaper system?

A higher hydrogen price makes each kilogram worth more, so the optimizer builds a larger electrolyzer to capture more surplus wind. The extra capacity runs fewer full-load hours, so the cost per kilogram, the levelized cost of hydrogen, goes up. Yet the added hydrogen revenue lowers the net cost of the whole system. The cost per kilogram and the system's cost move in opposite directions.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I extended NREL's REopt optimization model with hydrogen components, ran the analysis and did the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeNREL's REopt optimization model had no electrolyzer, hydrogen tank or fuel cell.What I didI extended REopt with these three components, with their costs, efficiencies, hydrogen sales and constraints, so it sizes and dispatches wind, battery and hydrogen equipment together.Why it matteredFour system configurations could then be compared in one mixed-integer model.
ChallengeA wind farm's value to the grid depends on firm output, not only on the energy it sells.What I didI set the model to deliver the largest stabilized output in every hour at the lowest life-cycle cost, and compared battery, hydrogen and hybrid storage on that basis.Why it matteredHybrid hydrogen and battery storage delivered the highest stabilized output of the four configurations.
ChallengeResults from one site and one weather year may not hold elsewhere, or as equipment costs fall.What I didI repeated the analysis with wind profiles from four ISO regions and with projected component costs to 2050.Why it matteredThe ERCOT site had the lowest costs but the highest curtailment, and falling costs led to larger electrolyzers and less curtailment.



Design choices

Fix the wind farm at its planned 253 MWAlternatives considered: optimizing wind capacity together with storageThe study asks how storage and hydrogen should be added to a planned farm near Snyder, Texas, so only those components are sized.



Method
Mixed-integer sizing and dispatch optimization for a 253-MW West Texas wind farm with ERCOT prices, with sensitivities to hydrogen price, region and future technology costs.


Key findings

In the Journal of Mechanical Design case study, adding an electrolyzer reduced total system cost by about 7%.
In the same study, using hydrogen storage with fuel cells reduced it by about 26% and sharply cut curtailment (the earlier TORQUE 2022 case reported about 9% and 30%).



Boundary conditions
Cost assumptions date from 2020–2023 and predate final federal hydrogen credit rules.


What it led to
I reused the extended model and added a concentrated-solar module to compare solar-hydrogen designs. Co-located solar and hydrogen plants

title: Rethinking the economics and flexibility of U.S. nuclear power through hydrogen integration and policy support
text:
Honglin Li, Jianqiao Huang, Bikash Poudel, Mucun Sun, Tyler Westover, Daniel Wendt, Jie Zhang
Nature Communications, vol. 17, article 7090, 2026.
Abstract
Nuclear power supplies reliable low-carbon electricity and high-temperature heat, but existing plants face growing pressure to operate more flexibly in markets with rising renewable penetration. Coupling nuclear reactors with hydrogen production through high-temperature electrolysis may improve flexibility and create additional value, yet its economic potential remains uncertain. Here we show that integrating nuclear generation with hydrogen production and ancillary service participation can substantially improve the economics and operational flexibility of nuclear energy systems. Using an hourly optimization model linked to lifecycle techno-economic analysis, we find that retrofitting existing reactors with high-temperature electrolysis increases average net present value from about -$1.06 billion to about $240 million without policy support, while expanding flexible output by more than 115 MW for most reactors. Policy incentives, cost reductions, and optimized market participation further strengthen the value of nuclear-hydrogen systems for reducing costs and supporting grid reliability.

title: The role of small modular reactors in powering data centers for a sustainable digital economy
text:
Roshni Anna Jacob*, Honglin Li*, Ali Mahboub Rad, Bikash Poudel, Yaoyu Li, Mucun Sun, Timothy R McJunkin, Jie Zhang
Cell Reports Sustainability, vol. 3, article 100820, 2026. Co-first authors
* Equal contribution.
Abstract
This paper presents a critical perspective on the potential of small modular reactors (SMRs) to address the rapidly increasing energy demands of the digital economy, particularly those driven by advancements in artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on expertise in techno-economic analysis and the modeling and control of advanced nuclear reactors and integrated energy systems, we explore the prospects for deploying SMR technology to power energy-intensive data centers. We examine practical implementation pathways and identify the key technical, regulatory, and operational challenges that must be addressed for effective integration. The SMR-data center discussion is grounded on SMR designs, deployment configurations, grid integration strategies, and interactions with data center cooling systems. This perspective aims to assess the potential of SMR-powered data centers as a scalable and forward-looking solution to escalating electricity demands, emphasizing their role in enhancing energy resilience and sustainability.

title: Optimal planning of co-located wind energy and hydrogen plants: a techno-economic analysis
text:
Honglin Li, Jubeyer Rahman, Jie Zhang
Journal of Physics: Conference Series, vol. 2265, article 042063, 2022.
Abstract
Green hydrogen produced using renewable electricity could play an important role in a clean energy future. This paper seeks to analyze the techno-economic performance of integrated wind and hydrogen systems under different conditions. A co-located wind and hydrogen hybrid system is optimized to reduce the total system cost. We have adopted and improved a state-of-the-art techno-economic tool REopt, developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), for optimal planning of the integrate energy system (IES). In addition to wind and electrolyzer components, we have also considered battery energy storage, hydrogen tank, and hydrogen fuel cell in the IES. The results show that (i) adding electrolyzers to the grid-connected wind energy system could reduce the total system cost by approximately 8.9%, and (ii) adding electrolyzers, hydrogen tank, and hydrogen fuel cells could reduce the total system cost by approximately 30%.

title: Techno-economic analysis for co-located solar and hydrogen plants
text:
Honglin Li, Juha Kiviluoma, Jie Zhang
2023 19th International Conference on the European Energy Market (EEM), pp. 1–6, 2023.
Abstract
Power-to-X technologies with flexible electricity consumption has the potential improve the utilization of variable power generation. Both concentrated solar power (CSP) and photovoltaic (PV) plants can be used to produce green hydrogen, utilizing high temperature electrolyzers (HTE) or low temperature electrolyzers (LTE), respectively. There have been limited studies examining the feasibility of co-locating solar and hydrogen plants from a techno-economic standpoint. This paper presents a detailed analysis and optimization to compare the economic feasibility of an integrated CSP and HTE system versus an integrated PV and LTE system. It is assumed that the steam generated by the CSP is solely directed towards HTE, while the electricity produced by the PV system is either supplied to the grid or directed towards the LTE system. The Renewable Energy Integration & Optimization (REopt) and System Advisor Model (SAM) frameworks developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) are adopted and modified to perform the analysis. The results of the case study indicate that the integrated CSP and HTE system is more economically feasible compared to the integrated PV and LTE system, mainly due to the lower cost of thermal energy storage.
