title: Towards sustainable integration: techno-economic analysis and future perspectives of Co-located wind and hydrogen energy systems
text:
Honglin Li, Jie Zhang
Journal of Mechanical Design, vol. 146, article 020903, 2024. Featured Article
Abstract
This paper presents a comprehensive study that focuses on the techno-economic analysis of co-located wind and hydrogen energy integration within an Integrated Energy System (IES). The research investigates four distinct cases, each exploring various configurations of wind farms, electrolyzers, batteries, hydrogen storage tanks, and fuel cells. To obtain optimal results, the study employs a sophisticated mathematical optimization model formulated as a mixed-integer linear program. This model helps determine the most suitable component sizes and hourly energy scheduling patterns. The research utilizes historical meteorological data and wholesale market prices from diverse regions as inputs, enhancing the study’s applicability and relevance across different geographical locations. Moreover, sensitivity analyses are conducted to assess the impact of hydrogen prices, regional wind profiles, and potential future fluctuations in component prices. These analyses provide valuable insights into the robustness and flexibility of the proposed IES configurations under varying market conditions and uncertainties. The findings reveal cost-effective system configurations, strategic component selections, and implications of future energy scenarios. Specifically comparing to configurations that only have wind and battery combinations, we find that incorporating an electrolyzer results in a 7% reduction in the total cost of the IES, and utilizing hydrogen as the storage medium for fuel cells leads to a 26% cost reduction. Additionally, the IES with hybrid hydrogen and battery energy storage achieves even higher and stable power output. This research facilitates decision-making, risk mitigation, and optimized investment strategies, fostering sustainable planning for a resilient and environmentally friendly energy future.

title: Real-time greenhouse gas emission intensity informed demand-side load regulation for power grid decarbonization
text:
Honglin Li, Gulai Shen, Soroush Senemmar, Ali Mehmani, Jie Zhang
Cell Reports Sustainability, vol. 2, article 100367, 2025.
Abstract
The US targets net-zero-carbon electricity by 2035, emphasizing the need for both supply- and demand-side strategies in the power sector. Our study focuses on demand-side carbon reduction via load regulation, using real-time greenhouse gas emission data to optimize electricity use without reducing overall consumption. Our multi-scenario analysis indicates significant potential for carbon footprint reduction by adapting strategies to specific grid characteristics. For example, California could have 32.58% more emission reduction with annual instead of quarterly optimization. In grids with diverse generation resources, expanding adjustment ranges from ±5% to ±8% can boost carbon reductions from 1.19% to 1.64%. Our results also reveal low greenhouse gas intensity fluctuation areas as more cost sensitive in electricity consumption than high greenhouse gas intensity fluctuation areas, providing essential insights for policymakers.

title: Quantifying the Cost of Delayed Energization (CoDE) for AI Data Centers
text:
Honglin Li, Buxin She
2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS), 2026. Accepted
Abstract
Grid interconnection has become a binding constraint on artificial intelligence (AI) data center development, yet existing planning frameworks do not price service that arrives later than planned. This paper develops the Cost of Delayed Energization (CoDE), a present-value framework that maps delayed information technology (IT) capacity to grid MW and MVA requirements and prices the delay separately for developers, ratepayers, and society. Two decision metrics, delay cost intensity and the break-even acceleration payment, make results comparable across project sizes, delays, and mitigation options. For a 300 MW-IT project delayed 36 months, private CoDE is 714 million USD, or 66.1 thousand USD per MW-IT-month, and committed-capital carrying cost keeps it above 1.0 billion USD at 60 months even as realization probability decays. A one-year natural-gas bridge over the same delay avoids 257 million USD of private cost while adding 25–68 million USD of expected climate damage, and the delay itself adds 25 million USD of ratepayer exposure. Because these third-party effects are smaller than the private values they are set against by factors of about four to thirty, the operative planning question is who should fund acceleration and how pathway externalities are compensated.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text: This guide is for researchers, students and analysts who build models of U.S. power markets, of large new loads such as data centers and electrolyzers, and of the clean firm supply that may serve them. It covers fifteen public datasets and open tools in five groups: grid operations and markets; generation, load and emissions; interconnection and planning; costs and technology; and modeling tools. Each entry says who publishes the source, what it covers, how to get it, what its terms allow (including whether you may redistribute what you download), and the pitfalls that tend to cost time. Where a pitfall comes from my own published work, the entry links the public documentation of the framework repository in which the step is written down; the others come from the publisher’s own documentation. As of 2 November 2026, every fact below was checked against the publisher’s official pages. Terms, versions and addresses change, so confirm them at the source before you rely on them. One naming note: on 1 December 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy changed the name of the lab known as NREL (National Renewable Energy Laboratory); it is now the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). Its tools and data now live on nlr.gov, and older nrel.gov links no longer resolve.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Grid operations & markets

ERCOT 60-day SCED and DAM disclosure reports
What it is. ERCOT, the grid and market operator for most of Texas, publishes resource-level dispatch, offer and award data once a 60-day confidentiality period has passed. The 60-Day SCED Disclosure Reports (NP3-965-ER) cover real-time security-constrained economic dispatch. The 60-Day DAM Disclosure Reports (NP3-966-ER) cover the day-ahead market.
Coverage. Both reports have run daily since 29 January 2011, with one ZIP package of CSV files per operating day. The SCED package includes separate files for generation resources, load resources and energy storage resources in SCED, at SCED-interval resolution. The DAM package includes energy bids and awards, resource data and ancillary-service offers and awards. ERCOT’s market reports index lists these alongside the shorter 2-day and 3-day disclosures.
Access.

Open the product page and download the daily ZIP files. ERCOT’s Disclosure Reports Column Definitions Guide, linked there, defines the columns.
For long histories, use the ERCOT Data Access Portal or the Public API (see the next entry).
Expect a lag of about 60 days. For example, ERCOT’s notices show that the report for operating day 27 June 2024 was posted on 26 August 2024.

License and terms. ERCOT’s Terms of Use let you use, reproduce and redistribute public content on two conditions: the content is not modified, and its copyright and other notices are kept. Raw data may go into your own compilations, charts and analyses without those notices. ERCOT does not warrant the accuracy of the data, and its name and logo need written permission. Redistribution: allowed for unmodified files; derived analyses allowed.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. ERCOT data follow Central Prevailing Time, so every spring has a missing hour and every fall a repeated one. On the long day, ERCOT labels the repeated hour separately from the normal one. My Texas hydrogen framework converts every series to one fixed-offset clock before aggregating, then reindexes it to a complete hourly axis.
From intervals to hours. Average each resource’s SCED intervals within each hour to get its energy for that hour. An hour without a record is missing, not zero. Fill only short gaps, resource by resource, before summing to zones; after summing, a silent resource is hidden by its neighbors.
Locations. Disclosure files identify resources by ERCOT name, not by county. The framework matches each one to its plant in EIA-860, which gives the county and from that the weather zone. The mapping table is kept under version control, and unmatched capacity is reviewed.
Capacity factors. The denominator should be the capacity actually operating in that hour, taken from commissioning dates; year-end capacity understates early-year capacity factors. Look at the maximum before any clipping: a value above 1 means a matching or capacity error.
Corrections. ERCOT sometimes reposts disclosure data. A March 2026 market notice, for example, announced supplemental files for a load-resource file affected from December 2025 to January 2026. Watch the market notices and re-download the affected days.

Used in. Hydrogen’s role in expanding renewable energy in Texas (TXH2). The full recipe and its checks are in the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


ERCOT prices, the Data Access Portal and the Public API
What it is. ERCOT’s public market reports, including prices, are available through three routes: the data-product pages on ercot.com, the ERCOT Data Access Portal for search and archives, and the ERCOT Public API.
Coverage. DAM Settlement Point Prices (NP4-190-CD) give day-ahead prices at resource nodes, load zones and trading hubs. Real-time settlement point prices (NP6-905-CD) are posted every 15 minutes. Bus-level DAM Hourly LMPs (NP4-183-CD) are a separate product. These nodal products have run since late November 2010. The product pages list only recent files; the DAM hourly LMP page, for example, keeps the last 30 days.
Access.

For a quick look, download recent files from the product page.
For history, search the Data Access Portal. Its search reaches back to 30 November 2023; older archives come as downloadable file packages.
For programmatic access, register on the ERCOT API Explorer and subscribe to the Public API product to obtain a subscription key. Then request an ID token with your account credentials; it is valid for one hour and cannot be refreshed. Send both the key and the token with every request, as the registration guide describes. Data through the API start on 11 December 2023.
Open-source clients such as gridstatus (BSD-3-Clause) wrap these steps. My nuclear–data-center framework retrieved ERCOT day-ahead hub prices with it.

License and terms. ERCOT’s API support page states that the same Terms of Use govern the API: unmodified redistribution with notices kept, and free use in your own analyses. Keep your API credentials out of scripts and repositories. Redistribution: as for the disclosure reports.
Known pitfalls.

Settlement point price or LMP. Prices at hubs, load zones and resource nodes, and prices at individual electrical buses, are separate products with separate report IDs. Choose the one for the location your site would face; the nuclear–data-center framework uses the day-ahead price at a hub.
15-minute prices. Average each hour’s intervals before joining them to hourly data. Check that every hour has its full set of intervals, and treat a missing interval as an error, not as a zero.
Negative prices. Keep them. A model that buys and sells at the grid should see hours in which exporting costs money.
Year length. After converting clocks, check that a normal year has exactly 8,760 rows. In a leap year, treat all series alike: remove the leap day from each of them, or keep all 8,784 hours throughout.
Units. Market prices are in $/MWh. Models that work in kW, such as REopt-based ones, need $/kWh, so divide by 1,000.

Used in. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center, with its smr-datacenter-cogeneration data pipeline; co-located wind and hydrogen, co-located solar and hydrogen and offshore wind–hydrogen O&M, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


PJM Data Miner
What it is. Data Miner, still called Data Miner 2 on many pages, is PJM Interconnection’s tool for its public market and operations data. It has a web interface and an API.
Coverage. Data are organized as feeds, each with its own definition, posting frequency and retention. Feeds include day-ahead and real-time hourly LMPs, five-minute real-time LMPs, settlement-verified LMPs, hourly load (preliminary, estimated and metered), load forecasts and generation by fuel type. Price feeds cover all bus locations, including aggregates.
Access.

The web interface needs no account. Choose a feed, set the dates, filter, and export to CSV.
For the API, create a PJM account, sign in to the API portal and obtain a key. A non-member must also confirm to PJM by e-mail that the data will be used only for internal business purposes. The steps are in PJM’s Data Miner API Guide.
Every API query needs a date filter, and a standard query is limited to about one year of data.

License and terms. Under the Data Miner terms of use, PJM members may republish data and non-members may not. PJM’s API guide adds that commercial use, including publishing data or making derivatives of it, requires PJM membership (at least Associate Membership). PJM’s API portal states that passing on Data Miner data, or anything derived from it, requires a Redistribution License issued by PJM. Non-members are limited to 6 data connections per minute (members to 600). Redistribution: not allowed without PJM authorization. In practice, publish your code and a download recipe, not the PJM data. The documentation of my supply-chain framework recommends the same approach for any source whose terms forbid redistribution.
Known pitfalls.

Two clocks. Feeds carry both Eastern Prevailing Time (_ept, which observes daylight saving) and UTC (_utc) timestamp columns. PJM recommends filtering and sorting on the same one. Pick one and convert once.
Archive rules. Hourly LMP feeds older than 731 days, and five-minute LMPs older than 186 days, move to an archive. Archive queries must stay within one UTC calendar year, must not span archived and recent data, and allow fewer filters. PJM’s example is that you can request all aggregates by pnode type, but not one specific pnode.
Preliminary and final values. Hourly load comes in preliminary, estimated and metered versions, and LMPs have settlement-verified feeds. State which version you used.
Throughput. At six connections per minute, a non-member’s bulk download of nodal history takes time. Plan it, and keep the raw files with their download dates.

Used in. Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants (NPPH2). PJM is one of the seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets in that study.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Generation, load & emissions

EIA-930 Hourly Electric Grid Monitor
What it is. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) collects hourly operating data from the balancing authorities (BAs) of the Lower 48 states on Form EIA-930. It publishes them through the Hourly Electric Grid Monitor.
Coverage. Hourly data for each BA: demand, demand forecast, net generation, total interchange and interchange with each neighboring BA. EIA aggregates them into 13 regions and a Lower 48 total. Data start on 1 July 2015. Net generation by energy source, subregion demand and EIA’s estimated CO₂ emissions start on 1 July 2018, and battery storage became a separate energy source on 1 January 2025.
Access. Use the dashboards, the six-month CSV files (balance, interchange and subregion), or the full-history workbooks for each BA and region. The files are under Download Data in the upper right of the Grid Monitor’s dashboard. The EIA API needs a free registered key and serves EIA-930 data from 1 January 2019 onward; older data are in the downloadable files. EIA’s About the EIA-930 data page is the best single reference.
License and terms. EIA’s copyright and reuse policy places its publications, as federal government works, in the public domain, and lets you use and distribute its data. EIA asks for an acknowledgment that names it and gives the publication date. Redistribution: allowed.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. Values are hour-ending. Each BA reports in a local time zone of its own choosing, and a few choices are unexpected: El Paso Electric reports in Arizona time and Idaho Power in Pacific time, for example. The six-month files carry both a local and a UTC end-of-hour stamp. My carbon-aware load framework works in UTC or local standard time, never in a clock that repeats an hour.
Daylight-saving days. These days have 23 or 25 hours, and EIA notes that they are often misreported, with duplicated, missing or mislabeled hours. Check them before anything else.
Raw, imputed or adjusted. EIA publishes BA-level data as reported, while its regional and national totals include imputation. The six-month files carry raw, imputed and adjusted columns side by side. Choose one deliberately and say which.
Revisions. Values can change after first release. My framework records the access date and a SHA-256 checksum of every downloaded file, so a result can be traced to the exact data used.
Zeros and negatives. An hour with zero demand is a reporting gap and should be treated as missing. My carbon-aware load framework clips negative net generation, such as pumping or station use, to zero and reports how many values were clipped.
Units. Emission intensity comes in lb CO₂/kWh. Converting to kg CO₂/MWh multiplies by 453.59237, so a result that is off by a factor of about 450 signals a unit mix-up.
Changing categories. New energy-source columns, such as battery storage from 2025, change the set of fuels. Map every year to one consistent set before comparing years.
Average, not marginal. EIA’s CO₂ estimates use annual average emission factors, so hourly intensities built from these data are averages. My studies that used them state this boundary explicitly.
Totals. Hourly totals can differ from EIA’s monthly and annual publications because coverage and methods differ. Compare annual totals with EIA’s published figures as a check.

Used in. Emission-intensity-informed load regulation (GHG), with the ghg-load-regulation data pipeline; SMR cogeneration for a hyperscale data center, for hourly grid carbon intensity.


EIA-860, EIA-860M, EIA-861 and EIA-923
What it is. These are EIA’s core surveys of U.S. power plants and utilities: generators (EIA-860, annual, and EIA-860M, monthly), utilities and retail sales (EIA-861), and generation and fuel (EIA-923).
Coverage.

EIA-860. Generator-level data on existing, proposed and retired units at plants of 1 MW or more, organized as operable, proposed and retired-or-canceled tabs. Annual files cover 2001–2025; the final 2025 data were released on 10 September 2026.
EIA-860M. The monthly status of existing and proposed generators. Monthly files run from July 2015 to September 2026; the September file was released on 23 October 2026.
EIA-861. An annual census of U.S. electric utilities: retail sales, revenue and customers by state, sector and balancing authority, plus net metering, demand response, service territories and more. Data cover 1990–2025, with the final 2025 data released on 7 October 2026. A monthly companion, EIA-861M, also exists.
EIA-923. Monthly and annual generation, fuel consumption, fuel stocks, fuel receipts and costs, and environmental data. Data cover 2001–2026; the latest monthly release covers August 2026, and the final 2025 data were released on 14 September 2026.

Access. Download ZIP archives of Excel workbooks from each survey page. Many series are also on the EIA API.
License and terms. Public domain, as for EIA-930. Redistribution: allowed, with credit to EIA.
Known pitfalls.

Preliminary and final values. EIA-860M capacities are preliminary estimates that EIA later corrects without specific notice. Early-release annual data are not yet fully validated. Monthly EIA-923 releases cover only the plants in the monthly survey (about 3,000); the final annual file adds the plants that report annually.
Planned is not committed. EIA notes that capacities reported for planned units are not commitments by the facilities.
Retirements. The Retired tab of the annual EIA-860 is not comprehensive. The monthly inventory tracks retirements back to 2002.
Location and timing. EIA-860 gives each plant’s county and each generator’s operating month and year. My Texas framework uses the county to place market resources in zones, and the operating dates to count capacity only from the hour it entered service.
QA. Before using hourly inputs, compare annual energy by zone and technology with EIA-923.

Used in. TXH2: EIA-860 for locations, capacity and storage, and EIA-923 for QA. See the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


IEA Energy and AI
What it is. The International Energy Agency’s special report Energy and AI (10 April 2025), its follow-up Key Questions on Energy and AI (16 April 2026), and the online Energy and AI Observatory. A further IEA report, Powering Artificial Intelligence (14 October 2026), deals with integrating data centers into power systems.
Coverage. Global and regional estimates of data-center electricity consumption and installed capacity, with projections to 2030 and 2035. The 2025 report has a Base Case and three sensitivity cases: Lift-Off, Headwinds and High Efficiency. The Observatory (last updated 16 June 2025) shows installed capacity by data-center type (enterprise, colocation and hyperscale), capacity by region, and a map of large data-center hubs.
Access. Read the reports online or download the PDFs; the Observatory is interactive.
License and terms. The report pages carry a CC BY 4.0 license. The IEA’s terms exclude standalone datasets, data explorers and data annexes from that license and place them under its terms for non-CC material. Redistribution: report text and figures allowed with attribution under CC BY 4.0. Data from the Observatory are not CC BY; check the IEA’s terms or ask the IEA before republishing them.
Known pitfalls.

Modeled, not metered. The IEA notes that there are no comprehensive global statistics on data-center electricity use. Its figures come from its own model, so treat them as estimates.
Cases and editions. The cases diverge widely by 2035. Always name the case and the publication you cite, and check whether a later IEA publication has updated the figure.
Granularity. The figures are national and regional. They cannot stand in for utility, interconnection or nodal load data.
Recording. In my framework for the cost of delayed energization (CoDE), values drawn from capacity outlooks become scenario values, such as case sizes, and never observations. Each one is recorded in a provenance table with its source and access date.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies. For the provenance rule, see the code-delayed-energization data pipeline.


SDWPF wind-farm SCADA dataset
What it is. SDWPF (Spatial Dynamic Wind Power Forecasting) is an open set of SCADA records from one wind farm of 134 turbines. It was released for the KDD Cup 2022 challenge and documented by its authors (Zhou et al.) in Scientific Data (2024).
Coverage. Records are at 10-minute resolution per turbine and include wind speed and direction, nacelle direction, blade pitch angles and active power. The full release, sdwpf_full, spans January 2020 to December 2021 (about 11.4 million records) with real timestamps, ERA5 weather variables and turbine elevations. The competition release, sdwpf_kddcup, holds the original 245-day file, which gives only a day index and time of day, with relative turbine positions.
Access. Download the CSV or Parquet files from figshare.
License and terms. The figshare record is licensed CC BY 4.0. Cite the Scientific Data article. Redistribution: allowed with attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Quality flags are defined but not applied. The dataset paper defines zero, missing, unknown and abnormal values. Power is unknown when it is at or below zero while wind speed exceeds 2.5 m/s, or when any pitch angle exceeds 89°; these cases often reflect curtailment or stops. The authors leave it to users to decide how to treat them.
Filter for your purpose. Forecast evaluation excludes those records. My multi-fidelity power-curve method keeps stops and curtailment on purpose, because its density-based sampling is meant to represent the turbines’ full operating behavior. It removes only rows with missing or non-finite values and negative power, and reports how many rows each rule removed.
Time. In the 245-day file, a timestamp is built as (day − 1) days plus the time of day.
Units and sensors. Check power units against the 1.5 MW turbine rating. Nacelle anemometers sit behind the rotor, which affects the wind-speed readings. Look for duplicate intervals after merges and for long runs of stuck values.

Used in. Multi-fidelity Gaussian processes for wind power curves, with the mfgpr-wind-power-curve data pipeline.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Interconnection & planning

LBNL Queued Up
What it is. Queued Up is Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s annual compilation of U.S. interconnection queues, produced with GridTracker. Interconnection queues list the proposed generation and storage projects that have asked to connect to the transmission grid.
Coverage. The 2026 edition covers requests through the end of 2025. It includes all seven ISOs/RTOs and 50 non-ISO utilities, which together hold about 98% of installed U.S. generating capacity. The Excel data file (updated May 2026) contains the project-level dataset, a codebook and summary tabs; a PDF slide deck (June 2026) and interactive maps accompany it. The scope is generation and storage seeking transmission-level connection. Load requests, distribution-connected projects and behind-the-meter projects are not included.
Access. Download the data file and slide deck from the Queued Up page. No registration is required.
License and terms. The data file is licensed CC BY 4.0, and the page asks that it be attributed to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and GridTracker. Redistribution: allowed with that attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Requests are not plans. Most requested capacity is withdrawn. Berkeley Lab reports that of the capacity requested in 2000–2020, only 13% had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025. My Texas study treated queued capacity as an upper bound, at a 100% completion rate, and applied completion rates as scenarios in the model.
Selection. The framework filters for requests whose status is active and whose proposed in-service date falls on or before the target year. It sums their capacity by county, then by zone, and converts it to output with the zone capacity factors.
Power and energy. Storage requests are usually stated in MW. If a model needs MWh, convert with an explicit storage duration and record that assumption.
Not a load queue. Queued Up does not track large-load requests such as data centers. Utility and ISO large-load disclosures are separate sources.
Editions. Figures change from one edition to the next. Cite the edition and the date of the data file.

Used in. TXH2, via the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


ReEDS
What it is. The Regional Energy Deployment System (ReEDS) is NLR’s open-source capacity planning and dispatch model of the U.S. power system. Its inputs folder is a documented collection of planning data, covering load, supply curves, transmission, plant characteristics, fuel prices, financing and state policies.
Coverage. The contiguous United States over multi-decade planning horizons. The latest release, 2026.09.21, was published on 30 September 2026. It represents the country as 90 model zones by default, each a group of counties that need not match a balancing authority area; release 2026.08.03 changed the default from 132 zones to these 90 (spatial resolution).
Access.

Clone github.com/ReEDS-Model/ReEDS. The earlier NatLabRockies/ReEDS-2.0 repository is archived.
Follow the documentation to set up the conda and Julia environments.
Large files, such as hourly demand and wind and solar profiles, are downloaded at run time from the hosts listed in inputs/remote_files.csv. Each input folder has a README that describes its sources.

License and terms. The code is BSD-3-Clause. ReEDS is written in Python, GAMS and Julia, and GAMS requires a commercial license; the documentation asks for a combined GAMS/CPLEX license. Small systems have been solved with an open-source solver, but the developers say that path is not actively maintained. The inputs are compiled from many sources. Redistribution: code allowed under BSD-3-Clause; for derived input data, check the terms of the original source first.
Known pitfalls.

Version pinning. Inputs change from release to release. Record the release tag and the identifiers of the remote files a run used.
Dollar years. The model documentation reports different inputs in different dollar years. Convert everything to one constant-dollar year before reusing it, as all my frameworks do.
Scope. Each model zone is treated as a copper plate, and capacity decisions have limited foresight unless intertemporal mode is used. The results are least-cost planning outcomes under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies.


NRC and DOE advanced-reactor licensing resources
What it is. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s public pages and records on licensing new and advanced reactors, and the Department of Energy’s Gateway for Accelerated Innovation in Nuclear (GAIN), which gives developers access to technical, regulatory and financial support.
Coverage.

Licensing pathways. Under 10 CFR Part 50, a plant needs a construction permit and then an operating license. Part 52 offers a combined license, early site permits and certified standard designs. The NRC’s licensing backgrounder explains both. Part 53, a technology-inclusive licensing framework based on risk insights, was published as a final rule on 30 March 2026 and took effect on 29 April 2026. It is optional; Parts 50 and 52 remain available. The NRC also lists proposed Part 57 requirements for microreactors.
Project status. The NRC publishes licensing dashboards for advanced-reactor applications under review. Its ADAMS public library holds more than three million documents released since November 1999.

Access. Everything is free. ADAMS has a public search, the dashboards are linked from the advanced-reactor page, and Federal Register notices are on govinfo.gov.
License and terms. The NRC’s site disclaimer treats its website as a U.S. Government work that is not subject to copyright and asks for credit when material is republished. Copyrighted third-party items on the site need the owner’s permission, and documents submitted by applicants may fall into that category. Redistribution: NRC-authored material allowed; check third-party documents first.
Known pitfalls.

Milestones are distinct. Acceptance of an application for review, completion of the safety and environmental reviews, the hearing, issuance of a construction permit, and authorization to operate are separate events. Under Part 52, operation is authorized only after the required inspections, tests and analyses are verified. Record which milestone a date refers to.
Cite the record. Use the ADAMS accession number (it starts with “ML”) or the Federal Register citation rather than a news report.
Pathway matters. The same design can be licensed under different parts of the regulations. Note the pathway when you compare schedules.

Used in. The smr-datacenter-cogeneration data pipeline lists public regulatory documents among the sources for reactor design parameters in the SMR cogeneration study.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Costs & technology

Annual Technology Baseline
What it is. NLR’s Annual Technology Baseline (ATB) is a yearly set of cost and performance estimates for electricity generation and storage technologies, with projections through 2050. A transportation ATB is published alongside it, and the electricity ATB pairs with NLR’s Standard Scenarios.
Coverage. The 2025 electricity edition was posted to the Open Energy Data Initiative (OEDI) in late August 2026. It covers capital cost, O&M, capacity factor, financial assumptions and levelized cost of energy by technology. Projections come in conservative, moderate and advanced versions, and there are separate financial cases, including an R&D-only case. The OEDI data lake holds the 2019–2025 editions.
Access. The data page links an Excel workbook, summary CSV and Parquet files on OEDI, Tableau workbooks, and the ATB-calc Python code. Read the disclaimer and the technical limitations first.
License and terms. The OEDI record is licensed CC BY 4.0. Cite the edition you use. Redistribution: allowed with attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Representative, not site-specific. The ATB leaves out site-specific resources, designs and regional labor and material costs. For a site-level cash flow, NLR points to SAM (see below).
Compare components. NLR’s guidance is that comparing capital cost, O&M and capacity factor directly is more reliable than comparing levelized costs.
Financial cases. The R&D-only projections reflect technology change alone, not short-term market swings, and separate cases include tax credits. Do not mix values from different cases.
Editions and errata. Values change between editions, and each edition has an errata page. My nuclear–data-center framework records the edition used, together with one constant-dollar year for every cost and price in a run.
Units. Convert each cost to the size unit the model uses (per kW of net output, per kWh of storage, or per kg/h of electrolyzer capacity) before use, not inside the model.

Used in. SMR cogeneration for a hyperscale data center (reactor, gas-plant and battery costs) and co-located solar and hydrogen (cost trajectories). See also the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


Cambium
What it is. NLR’s Cambium datasets are modeled hourly projections of the U.S. electricity sector through 2050. They are built from ReEDS capacity-expansion runs and production-cost modeling for a range of futures, as a companion to the Standard Scenarios. Metrics include long-run and short-run marginal emission rates, average emission rates and several marginal-cost measures. The latest release, Cambium 2024, is the fifth annual edition, documented in an April 2025 report.
Coverage. Hourly data for a series of solve years from 2025 to 2050. The underlying models represent the contiguous United States as 133 balancing areas. Summary workbooks use 18 regions and include levelization tools.
Access. Download the full datasets from the Scenario Viewer (Cambium 2024 project, Download tab) and the summary workbooks from the NLR Data Catalog.
License and terms. The Data Catalog’s dataset license allows free use and copying, provided the full notice appears in every copy and publications credit DOE, the laboratory and its operator; their names may not be used for endorsement. The Scenario Viewer’s disclaimer likewise asks for credit and provides the data as is. Redistribution: catalog workbooks may be copied with the notice. For the full datasets I found no separate redistribution grant, so link to the viewer.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. The timestamp field is in Eastern Standard Time and timestamp_local in local standard time. Both are hour-beginning and ignore daylight saving. Every year has 8,760 hours and starts on a Sunday, and leap days are dropped. Market and EIA data are usually hour-ending in local or prevailing time, so shift before joining.
Purpose. NLR designs Cambium for long-term, forward-looking analysis, not for historical accounting or real-time decisions. For the 2020s, it suggests observed data instead.
Costs are not prices. Cambium’s marginal costs can differ from market prices and should not be used as retail rates.
Small changes only. The data carry no elasticities, so the values become less reliable the larger the intervention being analyzed.
Average or marginal. Choose the emission rate that fits the question. My load-regulation and nuclear–data-center studies used average intensities from historical EIA data and state that boundary.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Modeling tools

REopt
What it is. REopt is NLR’s techno-economic optimization platform for sizing and dispatching energy systems at buildings, campuses, communities and microgrids. It is available as a web tool, as an API, and as the open-source Julia package REopt.jl, which is the optimization engine behind both.
Coverage. One year of operation, at hourly or finer resolution, for PV, wind, storage, combined heat and power, conventional generation and electrification options. Resource profiles come from PVWatts and the Wind Toolkit, and utility tariffs from the Utility Rate Database.
Access. The API is at version 3; versions 1 and 2 were decommissioned on 31 March 2024. It needs a free key from developer.nlr.gov, limited by default to 1,000 requests per hour. To use REopt.jl, add the REopt, JuMP and HiGHS packages in Julia. An NLR developer key is needed to fetch PV and wind resource profiles, and a separate key to fetch utility rates.
License and terms. REopt.jl is licensed Apache-2.0. The web tool and API are free. Redistribution: code allowed under Apache-2.0.
Known pitfalls.

Series length. Every time series must have exactly 8,760 values per time step per hour, so drop 29 February in leap years. REopt.jl rejects a load series of the wrong length.
Calendar year. Set the load year to the year of your data so that tariff periods line up with weekdays. Built-in reference building profiles default to 2017, a year that starts on a Sunday.
Units. REopt works in kW and $/kWh, so convert market prices from $/MWh.
Keys. REopt.jl reads its keys from environment variables. Keep them there, never in scripts or repositories.
Extensions. When I started my wind–hydrogen studies, REopt had no electrolyzer, hydrogen tank or fuel cell. I added them, and the reopt-hydrogen-framework documents that formulation.

Used in. Co-located wind and hydrogen, co-located solar and hydrogen and offshore wind–hydrogen O&M, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework.


SAM and PySAM
What it is. The System Advisor Model (SAM) is NLR’s free desktop application for the performance and financial modeling of energy technologies such as PV, wind, concentrating solar power and storage. PySAM is its Python wrapper.
Coverage. Simulations of one year at hourly or subhourly time steps, driven by a weather file and coupled to financial models. NSRDB solar data can be downloaded from within SAM, and other weather sources are listed on SAM’s site.
Access. Download SAM for Windows, macOS or Linux. Install PySAM with pip install nlr-pysam. The package was renamed from nrel-pysam, whose last release is 7.1.1. PySAM 8.0.0 (July 2026) matches SAM 2026.7.3 and supports Python 3.9–3.14. The documentation is at nlr-pysam.readthedocs.io.
License and terms. SAM is free, and its open-source code is licensed BSD-3-Clause, as is PySAM. Redistribution: code allowed under BSD-3-Clause.
Known pitfalls.

Version match. Each PySAM release is built against a specific SAM version, and default inputs can change between versions. Pin the version and record it with your results.
Renamed package. Requirements files that pin nrel-pysam stay on the 7.x line.
Same year, same weather. My solar–hydrogen framework runs the SAM plant model with the same year and weather file as the rest of the inputs. It divides hourly thermal output and parasitic load by the plant’s design thermal output, so the optimizer can scale the plant.
One clock. Align SAM output to the model’s calendar year and time-zone convention before joining it to market prices.

Used in. Co-located solar and hydrogen, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


HiGHS and linopy
What it is. HiGHS is an open-source solver for linear, mixed-integer and quadratic programs. It is a C++ library with interfaces for C, C#, Fortran, Julia and Python (highspy). linopy is a Python library, built on xarray, that writes linear, mixed-integer and quadratic models with labeled, N-dimensional variables and passes them to a solver.
Access. Install with pip install highspy; the current release is 1.15.1. Install linopy with pip, uv or conda-forge; the current release is 0.10.1. linopy does not work without a solver, so install at least one.
License and terms. HiGHS and linopy are both MIT-licensed. Commercial solvers that linopy can call, such as Gurobi or CPLEX, need their own licenses. Redistribution: allowed under MIT.
Known pitfalls.

MIP gap. The default relative MIP gap in HiGHS is 10⁻⁴. My frameworks set the gap explicitly (10⁻⁶) and document it.
Check the status. My frameworks stop with an error unless the solver reports an optimal solution, and some recompute the balance equations from the solution as a check.
Scale. Full-year, multi-zone or stochastic planning models can exceed what an open-source solver handles in practical time. The framework docs record where a commercial barrier solver was needed, and where a shorter horizon with hour weights served for screening.
Nonconvex terms. My supply-chain models use Pyomo with HiGHS. One bilinear variant needs a solver that handles nonconvex problems, so the framework offers an enumeration form that HiGHS can solve.

Used in. linopy with HiGHS: txh2-ercot-hydrogen, ghg-load-regulation, reopt-hydrogen-framework and smr-datacenter-cogeneration. Pyomo with HiGHS: supply-chain-microgrid-models.

Every item is checked against its primary source. Views are my own and do not represent my employer. This guide is reviewed each quarter; corrections are made in place and noted here with the date.
Corrected November 7, 2026: ReEDS’s coverage now gives the latest release’s default spatial resolution (90 model zones) in place of 133 model balancing areas.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text: For the next two decades, the U.S. power system will rest on three pillars: renewables, nuclear and natural gas. The more useful way to say it is that the system needs three jobs done (cheap energy, firm capacity and flexibility), and each fuel is good at some of them. Gas will lose weight over that period, but it will remain a pillar until at least 2050. And in this decade the scarcest job is not cheap energy but firm capacity that can actually connect to the grid.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text:
Three jobs, not three fuels
Today these three pillars already carry the system: in 2025, gas supplied about 41% of U.S. utility-scale generation, nuclear about 18%, wind about 11% and solar about 7% (EIA). Listing fuels, though, hides what each one is for.

Cheap energy. Wind and solar produce the cheapest megawatt-hours when they run, and they dominate what is being built: of the 86 GW planned for 2026, solar and batteries make up nearly 80% (EIA). I count geothermal here too. Fervo’s Cape Station in Utah, the first greenfield enhanced geothermal development to reach commercial operation, only did so this year (Fervo), so the contribution of next-generation geothermal is still ahead of us.
Firm capacity. Nuclear and gas run when the weather does not cooperate and when a large load needs power around the clock.
Flexibility. Batteries, hydrogen and flexible demand move energy in time. In my own work, hydrogen earned its place as a flexibility tool, not as a fourth pillar: in Texas, renewable hydrogen covered only a small share of industrial demand (International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, 2025), while at nuclear plants its value came from turning baseload output into a flexible product (Nature Communications, 2026).

I leave fusion out of this picture. It may matter later, but it will not shape planning decisions made this decade.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Gas: still a pillar, with less weight
text:
Gas: still a pillar, with less weight
The Energy Information Administration’s 2026 outlook projects that gas, solar and wind together supply about 80% of U.S. generation by 2050 in most of its cases (EIA, April 2026). I read that as confirmation that gas stays a pillar for the next two decades. I expect its weight to shrink, and its role to move from bulk energy toward firm capacity that backs up renewables and large new loads.
What no longer holds is the planning habit of assuming that a gas plant can appear whenever a model wants it. GE Vernova reports 122 GW of gas-turbine backlog and slot reservations, has sold delivery slots into 2032, and prices 2026 orders roughly 50% higher per kilowatt than 2025 orders (GE Vernova, Q3 2026). The supply chain is not broken, so the assumption still holds in part. But a turbine slot is now a constraint with a date on it.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Why now: the scarce job is firm capacity that can connect
text:
Why now: the scarce job is firm capacity that can connect
Data centers used about 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024, and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s reference case reaches 11.8% by 2030 (LBNL, 2025 update). That demand arrives faster than the grid can absorb it:

On the supply side, generation and storage projects built in 2025 spent a median of more than five years between their interconnection request and commercial operation, in the regions with data, and only 13% of the capacity that requested interconnection from 2000 to 2020 had been built by the end of 2025 (LBNL Queued Up). These queues cover new supply; they do not include load requests such as data centers.
The country built 322 miles of new high-voltage (345 kV and above) transmission in 2024 (Grid Strategies and ACEG).
PJM’s 2028/29 capacity auction cleared at its price cap and still fell about 6.8 GW short of its reliability requirement (PJM).

When connection is the bottleneck, waiting becomes a cost in its own right. In my work on delayed grid energization, an illustrative modeled case put the cost to the developer of a 300 MW (IT) data center waiting 36 months on the order of $0.7 billion in present value, and who ends up paying depended on how large-load tariffs are designed (NAPS 2026 study, CoDE framework).

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: The nuclear pillar starts with the plants we already have
text:
The nuclear pillar starts with the plants we already have
The fastest firm, carbon-free megawatts are often the ones already built. In a study of 42 U.S. reactors at 2024 prices, nearly all had negative net present value when run as baseload plants selling only electricity, without capacity payments or the 45U nuclear credit; adding hydrogen production and grid services, with the assumed hydrogen production credit of $3/kg for ten years, brought most of them above zero (Nature Communications, 2026). The same logic shows up in today’s news: DOE has offered up to $5 billion for uprates that add about 1.1 GW at eight existing plants (DOE), and retired reactors are being prepared for restart. New reactors are a different decision: for a reactor serving a hyperscale data center, I found that capital cost and policy, far more than operating choices, decide whether it beats grid supply (Energy Conversion and Management, accepted).

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Policy should pay for the service, not for one output
text:
Policy should pay for the service, not for one output
If the system needs three jobs, incentives should pay for the job a plant does. Today’s main clean-electricity credit pays per megawatt-hour generated. In the same data-center study, that design made it more expensive to use reactor steam for cooling, because every unit of steam sent to the chiller forgoes both electricity and its credit; an incentive meant to close a capital gap ends up discouraging the more efficient use of the plant. The tax law also treats the three jobs unevenly: wind and solar lose the main credits for projects placed in service after 2027 unless construction began by July 4, 2026, while nuclear, geothermal and storage keep them into the next decade (26 U.S.C. § 45Y). Paying for delivered services (energy, firm capacity, flexibility, and heat or cooling where it is used) would let each pillar compete for the job it does best.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text:
What would change my mind

If gas-turbine delivery times fall back to about three years and gas’s share falls much faster than EIA projects, gas is a bridge, not a pillar.
If enhanced geothermal reaches DOE’s cost goal at scale, it belongs among the firm-capacity sources as much as among the cheap-energy ones.
If large loads show verified, measured flexibility in the gigawatts, flexibility becomes a pillar in its own right and the firm-capacity gap shrinks.


Every item is checked against its primary source. Views are my own and do not represent my employer. Corrections are made in place and noted here with the date.
Corrected November 7, 2026: the geothermal milestone now names Fervo’s Cape Station, the first greenfield enhanced geothermal development to reach commercial operation; the interconnection-queue figures are identified as generation and storage projects; the delayed-energization cost is identified as an illustrative modeled case; and the nuclear result now states its baseline conditions (2024 prices, no capacity payments or 45U credit, and the assumed $3/kg hydrogen production credit for ten years).

Numbers and symbols

.gitignore
A file listing names and folders, such as keys and large raw data, that git add skips while they are untracked; it does not remove files already committed.
Learn in K8


95% confidence interval
A range worked out from the data by a method that, over many repeated samples, would contain the true value 95 times in 100.
Learn in M14



A

Absolute reference
A spreadsheet address with $ signs, such as $E$1, that stays the same when a formula is copied to other cells.
Learn in K7


Absorption chiller
A chiller driven by heat, such as steam or hot water, instead of an electric compressor; it uses a salt solution that absorbs and releases a refrigerant.
Learn in CF5


AC power flow (AC check)
A calculation of a network's voltages, currents and reactive power as well as its MW, from the alternating-current equations; it shows what a DC power flow or a first estimate leaves out.
Learn in A17


Additionality
Whether a purchase brings new clean generation that would not have been built otherwise, rather than claiming output that existed anyway.
Learn in A16


AFUE (annual fuel utilization efficiency)
The share of a furnace's fuel energy that leaves the furnace as heat over a heating season, under a standard test that leaves out duct losses and the fan's electricity.
Learn in F3


Agent-based model
A simulation in which many decision-makers, such as farmers or households, each follow their own rules, so that the system's behavior comes out of their choices.
Learn in CK-R


Aggregator
A company that enrolls many customers' devices, offers their combined response to a grid operator or utility, and shares the payment with the owners.
Learn in A7


Alkaline electrolyzer
An electrolyzer that uses an alkaline liquid electrolyte to carry ions between its electrodes, with operating limits that depend on the equipment design.
Learn in A16


Ancillary services
Services besides energy that keep the grid steady, such as reserves and frequency regulation; grid operators buy them separately from energy.
Learn in CF5


Annualized capital cost
A building cost spread into equal yearly amounts over the equipment's life, with interest, so it can be set against a year's revenue.
Learn in CF4


Annuity factor
What one dollar paid every year for a number of years is worth today, once each dollar is discounted.
Learn in K3


Anticipation
When people change their behavior before a program starts because they know it is coming.
Learn in M14


API key
A private code that identifies you to an online data service; treat it like a password and keep it out of shared files.
Learn in K8


Apparent power
The combined size of real and reactive power, the square root of MW² plus Mvar², in megavolt-amperes (MVA); a wire's heating follows it, not MW alone.
Learn in A17


Area median income (AMI)
The middle family income of an area, used to sort households into income bands such as 0-30% or 50-80% of it.
Learn in A13


Array
An ordered list or table of numbers; a linear program's costs c, rule table A and limits b are arrays.
Learn in B1


Assert
A line of code that stops a program with a message when a stated condition is false.
Learn in B2


Attributed emissions
The share of a grid's CO₂ assigned to one user, for example each MWh it uses times that hour's average emission factor.
Learn in CF6


Attributional analysis
An analysis that gives a product its share of today's burdens from average data, so the shares of all products add up.
Learn in A11


Audit trail
A record that lets someone follow a qualitative analysis from its raw material, such as interview notes, to each finding.
Learn in R5


Automatic generation control (AGC)
The grid operator's computer system that raises or lowers plants over minutes to bring frequency back to 60 Hz.
Learn in lesson 3


Autoregressive multi-fidelity model
A linear way to combine two sources: the accurate curve is modeled as a scaled copy of the rough curve plus a learned correction.
Learn in CF8


Average emission factor
An hour's CO₂ from all the plants that ran, divided by all the electricity used in that hour.
Learn in CF6


Average power
The energy used over a period divided by the length of that period.
Learn in lesson 1



B

Balancing
Keeping the power that plants make equal to the power that people use, at every moment.
Learn in lesson 0


Balancing authority
The organization that keeps supply and demand balanced, moment to moment, in its own part of the grid.
Learn in lesson 0


Balancing loop
A feedback loop with an odd number of negative links, which tends to oppose the change that started it; with long delays it can overshoot or swing back and forth.
Learn in F2


Baseline
An estimate of what a customer would have used without a demand-response event, against which the cut is measured.
Learn in A7


Baseline forecast
A simple rule, such as same hour yesterday, that any forecasting model must beat on the same hours to be worth using.
Learn in M10


Baseload operation
Operating a plant at a relatively steady output to supply the portion of demand that persists through the day.
Learn in CF4


Basis risk
The risk that the price where a plant sells differs from the price at which its contract settles, such as its node against a trading hub.
Learn in A2


Battery duration
How many hours a battery can discharge at its rated power: its energy in MWh divided by its power in MW.
Learn in N1


Battery margin
What a battery earns per megawatt-hour it discharges, after paying for the power it charged and the energy lost on the way.
Learn in A2


Benchmark
A case whose right answer is known in advance, from a hand calculation or an independent source, used to test a model.
Learn in R5


Benefit per ton
An estimate of the health harm, in dollars, avoided by not emitting one more ton of a pollutant from a given kind of source, averaged over where those sources are.
Learn in F11


Bias
The average signed miss of a forecast, showing whether it tends to run too high or too low.
Learn in lesson 4


Bidding zone (price zone)
An area of a power market in which every seller and buyer gets the same wholesale price for each trading period, as in Europe's markets.
Learn in F10


Billion cubic feet (Bcf)
A unit of natural-gas volume, a billion cubic feet; EIA often gives gas flows in Bcf a day.
Learn in X2


Binding constraint
A rule that holds exactly at the selected plan, with no room to spare; loosening it may or may not improve the best cost.
Learn in lesson 10


Boolean operators
AND, OR and NOT, the words that join search terms: AND narrows a search, OR widens it, NOT leaves terms out.
Learn in R2


Boundary condition (of a finding)
The place, time, data and assumptions a result holds under, stated next to it so readers do not stretch it further.
Learn in R8


Branch
A movable label on a line of commits, so a what-if can grow without changing the main line of work.
Learn in K8


Branch and bound
A search for the best whole-number plan that solves relaxations, splits on a fractional decision (off or on), and drops every branch whose bound cannot beat the best plan found.
Learn in M2


Break-even price
The sale price at which a project's net present value is exactly zero; when electricity is its only revenue, with the same costs, output and discounting, it equals the plant's levelized cost.
Learn in A1


Bridge power
Temporary on-site generation that serves part of a load until its grid connection is ready.
Learn in CF7


Btu (British thermal unit)
A unit of heat, the energy that warms one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit; one kilowatt-hour equals 3,412 Btu.
Learn in F5


Buffer (GIS)
The zone within a set distance of a map feature, such as everything within 1 km of a wind turbine.
Learn in R4


Building code
The rules a city, county or state sets for how new buildings must be built, such as insulation, wiring and safety.
Learn in F1


Building envelope
A building's outer shell, its walls, roof, windows and floor, whose insulation and air sealing set how fast heat leaks out.
Learn in A15


Bulk power system
The large power plants and the high-voltage transmission network that carry electricity over long distances, as distinct from the local distribution grid.
Learn in X1


Bus
A point of the network where plants, loads and lines meet, such as a substation; a network model has one balance rule per bus.
Learn in M1



C

CAIDI
Customer Average Interruption Duration Index: the average minutes to restore one interruption, SAIDI divided by SAIFI.
Learn in F6


Calibration (of a band)
A band is calibrated when it holds what it claims: a 90% band holds about 90% of new outcomes, overall and within groups that matter.
Learn in M9


Capacity
The most power a plant can produce at once, often called its nameplate size.
Learn in lesson 5


Capacity accreditation
The share of a resource's MW that a grid counts toward its adequacy target, judged by how much the resource lowers the risk of a shortfall.
Learn in A5


Capacity bound
The largest size a model is allowed to choose for a piece of equipment.
Learn in CF4


Capacity credit
The share of a plant's size that planners count on to meet the year's peak, judged by how much it lowers the risk of a shortage.
Learn in CK-M


Capacity expansion model
An optimization model that decides what to build, as well as how to run it, at least cost.
Learn in lesson 13


Capacity factor
The energy a plant actually made over a period, divided by the energy it would have made running at full capacity the whole time.
Learn in lesson 5


Capacity market
An auction, run ahead of time, that pays plants and other resources for being available, in an amount a planner sets, on top of energy prices.
Learn in A3


Capacity payment
Money a plant earns for being available to run when needed, as in a capacity market, apart from the energy it sells.
Learn in CF4


Capacity utilization
The energy a machine used or made over a year divided by its size times 8,760 hours, its average loading, so half power all year gives 50%, as full power for half the year does.
Learn in M11


Capital cost
The money spent to build a power plant, usually given per kilowatt of capacity, before it makes any electricity.
Learn in lesson 7


Capital recovery factor (CRF)
The share of a building cost that must be repaid each year, with interest, to pay it off over a given number of years.
Learn in lesson 7


Capital stack
The layers of money that pay for a project, such as senior debt, tax equity and the sponsor's equity, each with its own place in the order of payment.
Learn in X5


Capture price
The average market price a plant's output earns, each hour weighted by what the plant produced in it.
Learn in A3


Capture ratio
A market price averaged over the hours a plant produces, weighted by its output, divided by that price's average over all hours.
Learn in A2


Carbon budget
A cap on the total CO₂ emitted over many years, a limit on a stock rather than on one year's flow.
Learn in F2


Carbon capture and storage (CCS)
Capturing CO₂ from a source such as a chimney before it reaches the air, and storing it, usually deep underground.
Learn in X2


Carbon dioxide removal (CDR)
Taking CO₂ that is already in the air and storing it in trees, soils, rock, minerals or products.
Learn in X2


Carbon intensity
The CO2 emitted for each unit of electricity, for example in tonnes per megawatt-hour.
Learn in lesson 12


Carbon price
A charge per tonne of CO2 emitted, added to costs so that cleaner choices become relatively cheaper.
Learn in lesson 12


Carnot limit
The largest share of heat any heat engine can turn into work: 1 minus the cold temperature over the hot temperature, both in kelvin.
Learn in F4


Carrying cost
What money tied up in buildings or equipment costs while they earn nothing: the interest, or the return it could have earned elsewhere.
Learn in CF7


Cash flow available for debt service (CFADS)
A project's revenue minus its operating costs in a period: the cash that can pay the loan.
Learn in X5


Causal-loop diagram
A map of causes and effects in which every arrow carries a sign: plus if more of the cause brings more of the effect, minus if it brings less.
Learn in F2


Chain reaction
A run of fissions in which the neutrons from each split go on to split more atoms; a reactor holds it steady, with each generation as large as the last.
Learn in F5


Chance constraint
A rule required to hold with a chosen probability, for example at least a 95% chance of meeting a week's demand, rather than with certainty.
Learn in CF1


Checksum
A short fingerprint computed from a file's bytes, such as SHA-256, that changes if even one byte of the file changes.
Learn in K8


Choice experiment
A survey method in which people choose repeatedly between offers whose features vary, so that the weight of each feature can be estimated.
Learn in X6


Circuit breaker
A switch that opens by itself when it senses a fault, cutting the power to everything beyond it, and can be closed again.
Learn in F6


Clean clone
A fresh clone of a repository into a new, empty folder, run with only what the repository holds, so that no file left on your own machine can change the result.
Learn in K8


Clean-energy standard
A rule that a set share of the electricity sold in a year comes from sources the rule counts as clean; sellers prove it with certificates, each a record of one MWh from a counted source.
Learn in A12


Clearing price
The price at which supply meets demand in a market; in a uniform-price market, every seller that runs in that hour is paid it.
Learn in lesson 8


Clone
A complete new copy of a repository, with its files and its whole history.
Learn in K8


Cluster study
A study of every interconnection request in one window together, which finds the network upgrades the group needs and splits their cost.
Learn in A6


Clustering
Grouping similar items, such as days with similar demand and weather, so that one representative can stand for each group.
Learn in R2


Co-op (electric cooperative)
An electric utility owned by the members it serves, common in rural areas.
Learn in R1


Co-optimize
To choose several decisions together in one model, so each is set with the others in view rather than one after another.
Learn in CF5


Coefficient of performance (COP)
Heat a heat pump delivers divided by the electricity it uses; a COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity.
Learn in F3


Cogeneration
Making two useful products from one fuel or heat source, such as electricity and heat, steam or cooling, instead of making each separately.
Learn in CF5


Coincident peak
The most a group of customers draws in the same hour; it is lower than the sum of their own peaks when they peak at different times.
Learn in A15


Combined-cycle plant
A gas power plant that burns gas in a turbine and uses the hot exhaust to make steam for a second turbine, so it gets more electricity from the same fuel.
Learn in lesson 0


Commit
A recorded snapshot of a project's tracked files as they were staged, with a message, its author and time, and a link to the commit before it.
Learn in K8


Compound hazard
Two or more hazards striking at the same time, such as heat and drought, whose combined harm can exceed the sum of each alone.
Learn in A9


Concentrated solar power
Mirrors focus sunlight to heat a fluid; the heat runs a turbine or a process, and it can be stored for hours in tanks.
Learn in CF2


Concept matrix
A table with papers in rows and ideas in columns, coded by a stated rule, that shows what a literature covers and what it leaves out.
Learn in R2


Condenser
The part of a steam plant that cools the used steam back into water, so it can be pumped back to the boiler; most of the plant's waste heat leaves here.
Learn in F4


Condensing furnace
A furnace that recovers additional heat by condensing water vapor in its exhaust, with efficiency depending on its design and operating conditions.
Learn in A18


Conditional price
A price read from a linear program in which the on/off decisions are held fixed; it holds only for that commitment.
Learn in M2


Conflict of interest
A financial or other tie that could bias, or seem to bias, a researcher's work, and so must be declared.
Learn in R9


Confounding
When something other than the program, such as a second change at the same time, also differs between the groups and moves the outcome.
Learn in M14


Congestion
A power line carrying all it is allowed to, so cheaper power cannot reach where it is needed and prices can differ by location.
Learn in lesson 8


Congestion rent
What loads pay at their locational prices minus what generators are paid at theirs; in a DC model it equals the sum, over the full lines, of each line's shadow price times its flow.
Learn in M1


Consequential analysis
An analysis of what changes because of a decision, in the short run through how plants run and in the long run through what gets built.
Learn in A10


Consequential emissions
The change in what power plants actually emit because of a decision, as the grid re-dispatches; it is counted with marginal, not average, emission factors.
Learn in A7


Constraint
A rule every solution must obey, such as supply equals demand or no plant above its size.
Learn in lesson 10


Control rod
A rod of neutron-absorbing material that is pushed into a reactor core to slow the chain reaction, or pulled out to speed it up.
Learn in F5


Control variable
A measured trait, such as home size, put into a regression so that groups are compared at equal values of it; it cannot fix a difference nobody measured.
Learn in M14


Coolant
The fluid, such as water, helium, liquid sodium or molten salt, that carries heat away from a reactor core.
Learn in F5


Coordinate reference system (CRS)
The rule that ties map coordinates to places on Earth; some keep areas true, others keep distances, none keeps both everywhere.
Learn in R4


Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)
The world reference clock, with no daylight saving; EIA stamps its hourly grid data in it.
Learn in B2


Coordination cost
What it costs to enroll, meter, control and pay each device or customer in a program, whatever the device's size.
Learn in A7


Correlated failure
Many parts of a system failing together because they share one cause, such as extreme cold freezing plants and gas supply at once.
Learn in A9


Cost of capital
The yearly return an owner's lenders and investors require on money tied up in equipment; the real cost of capital leaves inflation out.
Learn in M5


Cost of saved energy
What a measure costs per unit of energy it saves: its extra cost spread over its life at a discount rate, plus any extra yearly cost, divided by the energy it saves each year.
Learn in A15


Cost of service
What it costs a utility to serve a customer or a class of customers: energy, plants, wires, meters and billing.
Learn in A4


Cost per tonne avoided
A measure's net yearly cost, its capital spread over its life plus upkeep minus the energy it saves, divided by the tonnes of CO2 it avoids a year.
Learn in A18


Cost surface
A map that gives the cost of building a line or a road through each cell, for example in dollars per km.
Learn in A19


Counterfactual
What would have happened without the change being judged; every saving or effect is measured against one.
Learn in N1


Coverage
The share of actual outcomes that land inside a forecast's band; on its own it rewards wide bands.
Learn in M10


CO₂e (carbon dioxide equivalent)
Greenhouse gases such as methane counted as the mass of CO₂ that would warm the climate as much over a set period, so they can be added up.
Learn in A16


CRediT contributor roles
A standard list of 14 names for what each author did, such as conceptualization (shaping the question), data curation (cleaning and documenting data) and formal analysis.
Learn in R9


Critical (of a reactor)
The steady state of a chain reaction, with a multiplication factor of exactly 1; it is a reactor's normal operating state, not an emergency.
Learn in F5


Critical load

Developer

Diff
A line-by-line list of what changed between two versions of a file, with removed lines marked minus and added lines plus.

Dispatch

Econometrics

Efficiency

A machine that uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Equipment, such as a battery, that takes in electricity at one time and gives it back later, with some losses.

A catalog number that names one coordinate system exactly, such as EPSG:4326 for latitude and longitude in degrees.

A way to trace a trade-off by optimizing one goal while capping the other, then moving the cap step by step.

A map projection that keeps areas true, at the cost of shapes and distances; Albers equal-area (EPSG:5070) is the usual one for the contiguous U.S.

Ethics board (IRB)

Evidentiary hearing
A formal hearing at which the parties present their evidence and question each other's witnesses before the commissioners.

Ex-post review

Exajoule (EJ)

Exogenous

Expected unserved energy
Demand left unmet, averaged over many simulated years, in MWh a year: an amount of energy, unlike a load's size in MW.

The long-run average of an uncertain quantity: each possible outcome multiplied by its chance, then added up.

F

Falsification statement

Fast frequency response
Power from batteries or other inverter-based resources delivered within a fraction of a second of a frequency drop.

Feature

Final energy

The splitting of a heavy atom, such as uranium-235, into two smaller atoms when it absorbs a neutron, which releases heat and a few new neutrons.

Fixed charge

Land mapped as likely to flood; in the U.S., FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area is land with at least a 1% chance of flooding in any year.

How far ahead of the moment it is made a forecast looks, such as one hour or one day.

Frozen telemetry

Fuel assembly

Fuse

G

Gas reformer
A plant that makes hydrogen from natural gas and steam, releasing carbon dioxide unless it is captured.

Gigawatt (GW)

GIS (geographic information system)

Governor

Hydrogen made by electrolysis with renewable electricity, such as wind or solar power, rather than from natural gas.

H

Git's name for the commit you are on now; usually it points at a branch label, which points at that commit.

Horizon

I

A utility charge that varies with household income, such as a fixed charge set in a few income tiers.

Inertia
Energy stored in the spinning machines of a power grid; it slows a fall in frequency but cannot stop it.

Inflation

Islanding

J

Job-year
One person working full time for one year; 100 workers for six months make 50 job-years.
Learn in F8



K

A smooth estimate of where data points are dense, made by placing a small bump on every point and adding them up; sampling from it keeps the data's shape with fewer points.

Kilowatt (kW)
A unit of power equal to 1,000 watts.

Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
The unit of energy on a household electricity bill: one kilowatt kept up for one hour.

kW-DC

L

Latin hypercube sampling
