Learn in M5


Root mean square error (RMSE)
The square root of the average squared miss, in the units of the quantity; large misses count more than in the mean absolute error.
Learn in M9


Round-trip efficiency
The share of the energy put into storage that comes back out.
Learn in lesson 9


Run-of-river plant
A hydro plant with little or no reservoir, so it makes what the river's flow brings at the time.
Learn in F4


Running cost
What it costs a plant to make one more megawatt-hour, mostly fuel, leaving out the cost of building it.
Learn in lesson 0



S

SAIDI
System Average Interruption Duration Index: the minutes without power the average customer has in a year, customer-minutes divided by customers served.
Learn in F6


SAIFI
System Average Interruption Frequency Index: the number of sustained interruptions the average customer has in a year, total customer interruptions divided by customers served, so a customer interrupted twice counts twice.
Learn in F6


Sankey diagram
A flow diagram in which each band's width is the amount of energy it carries, so what flows in and out of every box can be read and compared at a glance.
Learn in F10


SCADA records
The operating records a wind farm's control system logs for each turbine, such as ten-minute averages of wind speed and power (supervisory control and data acquisition).
Learn in M9


Scale (of an energy system)
A level of an energy system, from one device or plant to a whole nation, set apart by who decides what and by the physics a model of it needs.
Learn in F1


Scarcity price
A wholesale electricity price that rises when supply or operating reserves are scarce, reflecting the value of meeting demand or maintaining reserves.
Learn in F2


Scenario
A coherent what-if set of a model's inputs, such as a 36-month wait; a scenario may be given a probability, though this lesson gives none.
Learn in M7


Scenario (one possible future)
One possible future of a model's uncertain inputs, such as how much planned wind and solar gets built and how fast demand grows; each scenario has a chance.
Learn in CF3


Scenario tree
A picture of a decision under uncertainty: a choice made now at the root, then one branch for each way the future may turn out, each with its chance.
Learn in M8


Scientific notation
A way to write a number as a value at least 1 and less than 10, times a power of ten, so very large and very small numbers are easy to compare.
Learn in K1


Scope 1 emissions
Emissions from sources inside the boundary being counted: a company's own boilers and vehicles, or, for a city, fuels burned inside its border.
Learn in A18


Scope 2 emissions
Emissions from the grid electricity, steam, heat or cooling that a company buys or a city uses, counted at the plants that make it.
Learn in A10


Scope 3 emissions
Other emissions that happen outside the boundary because of activities inside it, such as electricity lost on the wires that bring a city its power.
Learn in A18


Screening estimate
A quick estimate from stated assumptions and coefficients a reader can change, used to compare options, not to predict outcomes.
Learn in A13


Scrubber
Equipment that sprays a wet or dry chemical such as limestone through a plant's exhaust to capture most of its sulfur dioxide.
Learn in F11


SDWPF dataset
An open dataset of one wind farm's ten-minute operating records (SCADA), shared for research on wind power forecasting.
Learn in M9


Search string
The words and operators (AND, OR, quotation marks) typed into a literature database to find papers.
Learn in R10


Sector coupling
Linking energy carriers such as electricity, hydrogen and heat through devices that convert one into another, so that one carrier's supply and price affect the others.
Learn in M4


Selection bias
A false effect from who joins: those who take up a program differ from the rest in a way the comparison does not remove (difference-in-differences removes a fixed gap, not a different trend).
Learn in M14


Self-organizing map
A clustering method that places similar items, such as days, in neighboring cells of a small grid.
Learn in R2


Sensitivity analysis
Changing a model's inputs one at a time and re-solving, to see which inputs the answer depends on.
Learn in lesson 11


Service level
The share of cases in which a rule must hold, such as meeting store demand in 95 of every 100 weeks.
Learn in M5


Service voltage range
The voltage a utility keeps at a customer's meter in normal operation; in the U.S., ANSI C84.1 Range A, 114 to 126 V on a 120 V service (0.95 to 1.05 per unit).
Learn in A17


Setback
The least distance a project must keep from a home, road, line or other feature, usually set by local rules.
Learn in A19


Settlement (in a regulatory case)
An agreement among some or all parties to a case on how it should end, filed for the commission's decision.
Learn in X4


Shadow price
How much the best total cost would change if one rule were loosened by one unit; for the rule that supply equals demand, it is the price of one more megawatt-hour.
Learn in lesson 11


Sharpness (of a forecast band)
How narrow a forecast's bands are, on average; narrower is better only if the bands still hold what they claim.
Learn in CF8


Simplex method
A way to solve linear programs by moving from corner to neighboring corner of the feasible region, never making the goal worse, until no neighbor is better.
Learn in lesson 11


Site control
Proof that a project owns, leases or has the right to use the land it would be built on.
Learn in A6


Skill score
How much smaller a forecast's error is than that of a simple baseline such as persistence.
Learn in lesson 4


Snowballing
Finding papers from one you already have: backward through its references, forward through the works that cite it.
Learn in R2


Software environment
The language, packages and versions a program runs with, built from a lock file so that a rerun uses the same ones.
Learn in K8


Solver
Software that searches for an optimization solution and reports whether it is optimal, infeasible or unbounded, or stops at a time or other limit with or without a feasible solution.
Learn in lesson 11


Spare capacity (headroom)
The MW a substation or line can still take for a new load or plant without an upgrade.
Learn in A19


Spatial resolution
The size of a raster's cells: finer cells show smaller features, such as a setback, but need more data and more computing.
Learn in A19


Special ordered set (SOS2)
A rule in a mixed-integer program that lets at most two neighboring points of a curve be used, so the model can follow a curved line by joining straight pieces.
Learn in CF5


Spent fuel
Fuel that has been used in a reactor and taken out; it is solid, highly radioactive and still warm, and is kept first in water pools, later in dry casks.
Learn in F5


Spillover
When a program also changes the comparison group, for example neighbors copying a habit or projects moving across a border.
Learn in M14


Sponsor equity
The developer's or owner's own money in a project: paid last, so it carries the most risk and keeps what is left.
Learn in X5


SPP (Southwest Power Pool)
The regional grid operator that runs the transmission grid and wholesale electricity market across much of the central U.S.; the course's hourly data come from its area (EIA-930).
Learn in R8


Staged energization
Switching on part of a large load's grid service early and the rest later, as the grid becomes ready.
Learn in CF7


Staging area
Git's list of changes picked for the next commit: git add puts a file's current version there.
Learn in K8


Stakeholder
A person or group affected by a study or the decision it informs, or able to affect it.
Learn in R9


Standard deviation
A measure of spread: roughly, how far a typical value lies from the mean.
Learn in B2


Standard error
How far an estimate from a random sample typically lands from the value for the whole set; it shrinks as the sample grows.
Learn in K5


Standing loss
Energy a store loses while it waits, used or not, such as heat leaking from a hot tank; it grows with time, unlike the loss of each charge and discharge.
Learn in A8


Start-up cost
The fuel and wear spent to bring a plant from off to on, paid once per start.
Learn in M2


Start-up time
How long a plant takes to go from shut down to full output; the ramp rate is how fast it changes output once running.
Learn in F4


State of charge
The energy a battery holds at a given moment, in MWh; it links each hour of a storage schedule to the next.
Learn in lesson 9


Steam generator
A heat exchanger in which hot water from a reactor's sealed loop boils the water of a second, separate loop into steam.
Learn in F5


Steam turbine
A turbine spun by high-pressure steam from a boiler or another heat source.
Learn in F4


Stock
An amount that builds up or drains over time, such as water in a reservoir, energy in a battery or CO₂ emitted so far.
Learn in F2


Storage link (between periods)
In a model of representative periods, the energy stored at the end of one period carried into the next, so storage can move energy across days or seasons.
Learn in R2


Stranded cost
Money already spent on equipment that is no longer used as planned, such as grid upgrades built for a load that never arrives.
Learn in CF7


Stress test
Running a system model through a severe event on purpose, to see what breaks and what a defense would change.
Learn in A9


Structural uncertainty
Doubt about how a model is built (its equations, time steps and what it leaves out), which sampling its inputs cannot reveal; compare model forms instead.
Learn in R6


Stylized network
A simplified, made-up network built to show how a model behaves, with invented distances and costs rather than a real company's map.
Learn in CF1


Substation
A fenced yard of transformers, breakers and switches where the grid changes voltage and where feeders start.
Learn in F6


Substitution method
A rule for counting primary energy in which each MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal power plant would burn to make it.
Learn in F10


Suitability score
A cell's or a site's weighted score in a siting screen, here from 0 to 100: a ranking under stated weights, not a cost and not a verdict.
Learn in A19


Sunk cost
Money already spent that no choice made now can change, such as what an existing plant cost to build; it drops out when options are compared.
Learn in CF4


Supply diversity
How evenly the energy supply is spread over different sources, so that losing one does not lose most of it.
Learn in A22


Supply stack
All the offers to sell power in one hour, lined up from the cheapest to the most expensive.
Learn in lesson 8


Supply-chain tier
One level of a supply chain, such as factories, then warehouses, then stores: a three-tier chain has all three, a two-tier chain two of them.
Learn in CF1


Surrogate model
A cheap stand-in for a model or measurement that is costly to run, fitted to a few samples and then used in its place.
Learn in M9


Synchronous grid
A connected AC network whose generators and other equipment run at one shared electrical frequency; the Lower 48 states have three main ones, called interconnections.
Learn in F1


Synthetic data
Invented values made to look realistic, used in place of real records so that a model can be shown and shared.
Learn in CF1


Synthetic sample
A few invented records with the same columns and realistic values as data that cannot be shared, so others can run the code without the real data.
Learn in R9


System boundary
The line that decides which parts, costs and emissions a study counts and which it leaves out.
Learn in N1



T

Target-seeking scenario
A scenario that starts from a goal, such as a carbon budget, and works out what it would take to meet it; the IEA calls this kind normative.
Learn in A20


Tariff
The rule for calculating electricity bills: fixed charges, prices per kWh, or both.
Learn in A22


Tax base
The total value a local government can tax, such as the assessed value of homes, businesses and power plants in a county.
Learn in A13


Tax equity
Money from an investor with a large tax bill, put into a project in exchange for most of its tax credits and depreciation, plus some cash.
Learn in X5


Techno-economic analysis (TEA)
Estimating what a technology costs and earns from its engineering design, its prices and its operating pattern.
Learn in R10


Techno-economic optimization
A model that compares equipment sizes and ways of running them by both their performance and their cost, and picks the best for a stated goal.
Learn in F7


Technology readiness level (TRL)
A scale from 1 (basic principles described) to 9 (proven in operation) for how mature a technology or method is.
Learn in X2


Telemetry
Measurements sent automatically from plants and substations to the grid operator.
Learn in B2


Temperature lift
How far a heat pump raises heat: its delivery temperature minus its source temperature, in kelvin (a difference of 1 K equals 1 °C).
Learn in A15


Terawatt-hour (TWh)
A unit of energy equal to a billion kilowatt-hours, used for the yearly electricity use of regions and countries.
Learn in lesson 1


Thermal rating
The most current, or MVA at the line's voltage, that a line or transformer can carry before its wires get too hot and sag.
Learn in A17


Thermal storage
Storing energy as heat, for example in tanks of hot molten salt, to use it hours later.
Learn in CF2


Tie rule
A stated way to pick one answer when several plans cost exactly the same, usually tiny costs that are left out of the reported results.
Learn in SB3


Time slice
A group of hours, such as winter nights, that a planning model treats as one, weighted by how many hours it stands for.
Learn in SB4


Time step
The length of one step in a model or dataset, such as five minutes, an hour or a year.
Learn in R3



Time-of-use tariff
A retail electricity price that changes with the hour of the day, higher at peak times and lower off-peak.
Learn in A4


Time-series aggregation
Shrinking a long series, such as a year of hours, to a few representative periods that a model can solve quickly.
Learn in R2


Tolling agreement
A contract in which the buyer pays the owner of a plant a fixed fee for the right to run it, and keeps what it earns.
Learn in A2


Ton of coal equivalent (tce)
An energy unit equal to the heat in one metric ton of standard coal, fixed by convention at 29.3076 GJ; China's energy statistics count in it.
Learn in F10


Ton of oil equivalent (toe)
An energy unit equal to the heat in one metric ton of crude oil, fixed by convention at 41.868 GJ; ktoe is a thousand of them, Mtoe (Brazil's Mtep) a million.
Learn in F10


Tornado chart
A chart that ranks inputs by how far a result moves when each input is swung from a low to a high value, one at a time.
Learn in lesson 7


Tracked file
A file Git already knows, because it is in the last commit or the staging area; a new file stays untracked until git add.
Learn in K8


Trading hub
A pricing point where many contracts are settled, priced as an average over many nodes of the grid.
Learn in A2


Transactive energy
Buying and selling electricity among many small participants, such as homes and firms with their own generation, as well as with the grid.
Learn in A7



Transfer
A payment that moves money from one group to another, such as a carbon payment to the government or a credit to a plant owner, without using anything up.
Learn in A12


Transformer
A device with two coils that raises or lowers an alternating voltage, such as from 18 kV to 345 kV at a plant or from 12.47 kV to 240/120 V near a home.
Learn in F6


Transmission
The high-voltage part of the grid (115 to 765 kV in the U.S.) that carries power over long distances between plants, regions and substations.
Learn in F6


Transport model
A network model in which each link can carry any flow up to its limit, with no power-flow physics: power goes where the cheapest routes allow.
Learn in SB2


Triangulation
Checking a finding against a second source or a second method, so that it does not rest on one kind of evidence alone.
Learn in CR


Truncated axis
A chart axis that starts above zero; on a bar chart it makes differences look larger than they are.
Learn in R8


Turbine
A machine whose blades are pushed round by moving gas, steam, water or wind, turning a shaft.
Learn in F4


Turbine crossover
The pipe that carries steam from a high-pressure turbine to a low-pressure turbine; steam taken there has already done part of its work.
Learn in CF5


Two-stage stochastic program
An optimization model that chooses the here-and-now decisions and each branch's recourse together, to minimize the expected cost over all branches.
Learn in M8



U

Unbounded
Said of a model whose goal can improve without limit, which usually means a rule is missing.
Learn in lesson 10


Unbundling
Separating the grid from the making and selling of electricity, so that different companies, or legally separate parts of one, run each.
Learn in F10


Under-frequency load shedding
Relays that automatically disconnect blocks of customers when the frequency falls to a set level, to save the rest of the grid.
Learn in lesson 3


Unit commitment
Deciding which plants are on in each hour, before deciding how much each one produces.
Learn in lesson 11


Unserved energy
Demand that could not be met, so some customers lost power.
Learn in lesson 0


Uplift payment
A payment outside the market price that covers costs a scheduled plant cannot recover at the price, such as start-up and no-load costs; also called a make-whole payment.
Learn in M2


Uprate (of a line or link)
Raising the most power a line or link may carry, for example with new conductors or a second circuit.
Learn in SB2


Uranium-235
The form of uranium whose atoms split easily when they catch a slow neutron; natural uranium holds only a small share of it.
Learn in F5


Useful energy
Energy a device delivers in the wanted form, such as heat, light or motion; a heat pump's delivered heat includes heat drawn from the outdoor air, not only the energy bought.
Learn in F3


Utility-scale
Large enough to sell power to the grid; in EIA's statistics, plants of at least 1 MW.
Learn in R8


UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator)
A set of 60 north-to-south zones, each a flat map in meters that keeps distances close to true inside the zone.
Learn in R4



V

Validation
Checking that a model represents the real system well enough for the question it is used to answer.
Learn in B3


Value of coupling
How much cheaper a system is with devices that link its carriers than with each carrier supplied on its own, judged as a difference of optimal costs.
Learn in M4


Value of information
How much a decision-maker would gain, on average, by learning an uncertain quantity before deciding; its upper limit is the value of a perfect forecast.
Learn in R6


Value of lost load
What a customer loses when power is cut, per hour or per kWh not delivered; it differs by customer and by how long the outage lasts.
Learn in A14


Value of the stochastic solution (VSS)
How much the stochastic program's plan saves, in expectation, against the plan built for the average future.
Learn in M8


Variable O&M
Operation and maintenance costs, apart from fuel, that grow with every megawatt-hour a plant makes.
Learn in lesson 7


Variable renewables
Wind and solar power, whose output follows the weather: they can be turned down but not up.
Learn in lesson 0


Variogram
A measure of how much values at two places differ, on average, as a function of the distance between them; here, across a wind plant's turbines.
Learn in CF8


Vector
An ordered list of numbers, such as a plan's outputs, in which the position of each number carries its meaning.
Learn in K6


Verification
Checking that a model's equations and code implement the intended model correctly, with tests such as units, the energy balance and hand-solved cases.
Learn in B3


Version control
Keeping selected recorded versions of a project's files, with who changed what and why, so any recorded version can be compared or brought back.
Learn in K8


Version pin
A line such as pandas==2.2.3 in requirements.txt that asks the installer for one exact version of a package.
Learn in K8


Vertically integrated utility
An electric utility that owns and runs the power plants, transmission and distribution in its service territory, as Kansas's investor-owned utilities do; its rates are approved by the state regulator.
Learn in F9


Vintage
The year a plant was built: in a multi-decade model each vintage keeps its own cost and runs until its life ends.
Learn in SB4


Virtual power plant
Many small devices, such as batteries, thermostats and chargers, controlled together and offered to the grid as one resource.
Learn in A7


Voltage
The electrical push that drives current through a wire, measured in volts (V); 1 kilovolt (kV) is 1,000 V.
Learn in F6


Voltage angle
How far the alternating voltage at one bus runs ahead of the voltage at the reference bus, whose angle is set to zero; in DC power flow a line's flow is proportional to the angle difference across it.
Learn in M1



W

Wait-and-see problem
The planning problem solved as if the future were known: one best plan for each branch, which no real planner can choose in advance.
Learn in M8


Waste heat
Heat a power plant cannot turn into electricity and releases to the air or to cooling water.
Learn in F4


Water consumption
Water taken and not returned, mostly lost to evaporation, so it is no longer available downstream.
Learn in A11


Water withdrawal
Water taken from a river, lake or aquifer, of which the part not returned is consumption; how much returns depends on the cooling system.
Learn in A11


Watt-hour (Wh)
A unit of energy: one watt kept up for one hour; 1,000 Wh make one kilowatt-hour.
Learn in lesson 1


Weather zone
One of the areas into which a grid operator divides its region for weather and demand forecasts; ERCOT has eight.
Learn in CF3


Weatherization
Air sealing, insulation and similar work on a building's shell that cuts the heat it loses, so it needs less heating.
Learn in A18


Web Mercator
The projection most web maps use: good for viewing, but it stretches distances and areas more the farther a place is from the equator.
Learn in R4


Weibull distribution
A curve often used for the share of a year's hours at each wind speed; its shape k (no unit) sets how spread out the speeds are, and its scale c, in m/s, sets how high they run.
Learn in CF8


Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
The blended return a project must pay its lenders and its owners, used as the project's discount rate.
Learn in lesson 7


Weighted overlay
Combining several criterion maps cell by cell: each criterion is scored from 0 to 1, multiplied by its weight, and the results are added into one suitability map.
Learn in A19


Weighted sum
A way to combine several goals into one score by adding them up, each multiplied by a weight.
Learn in lesson 12


Well-to-gate
An emissions boundary from producing the inputs, such as gas or electricity, to hydrogen leaving the plant; delivery and use are outside it.
Learn in A16


Wet-bulb temperature
The lowest temperature evaporating water can reach in the air at hand, which combines heat and humidity; when it is high, chillers and cooling towers reject heat less well and deliver less, which is called derating.
Learn in CF5


Wholesale price
The price at which electricity is traded between power plants and the companies that sell it to customers, often set hour by hour.
Learn in lesson 8


Wildfire safety shutoff
A utility switching off power lines in dry, windy weather so that they cannot start a fire; the customers on those lines lose power.
Learn in A9


Willans line
A straight-line rule for a turbine's steam use against its output; here it gives the electricity lost for each unit of steam taken out of the turbine.
Learn in CF5


Winterization
Protecting power plants and fuel supply against freezing, with insulation, electric heaters on exposed pipes (heat tracing), enclosures and cold-weather procedures.
Learn in A9



X
No terms in this group.


Y
No terms in this group.


Z
No terms in this group.
